G5A_ALGEBRA_001.questionText: Meera thinks of a number n. She adds 5 to it, multiplies the result by 3, and then subtracts the number she first thought of. Which expression shows her final answer?
hints: Write down what Meera has after each action, one at a time. Use brackets when a whole result is multiplied.
After adding 5 she has n + 5. Now the whole of this is multiplied by 3. Write that with brackets, then open the brackets.
Similar problem: think of a number m, add 2, multiply the result by 4, then subtract m. That is 4(m + 2) − m = 4m + 8 − m = 3m + 8.

stepByStep.text: After adding 5, Meera has n + 5.
She multiplies the whole result by 3, which gives 3(n + 5). Both parts are multiplied, so this is 3n + 15.
She subtracts the number she first thought of: 3n + 15 − n.
3n − n is 2n, so her final answer is 2n + 15.

misconceptions.A: Here only the n was multiplied by 3. The 5 was added before multiplying, so it is multiplied by 3 as well.
misconceptions.B: Yes! 3(n + 5) is 3n + 15, and taking away n leaves 2n + 15.
misconceptions.C: This stops one action early. Meera still has to subtract the number she first thought of.
misconceptions.D: The last action takes n away. 3n − n is 2n, not 4n.

G5A_ALGEBRA_002.questionText: A rectangular sheet of card is 4p cm long and 3p cm wide. A square of side p cm is cut away from one corner. What is the perimeter of the piece of card that is left?
hints: Picture walking all the way round the edge of the new shape. Some edges have gone, but some new edges have appeared.
Start with the perimeter of the whole rectangle: 2 × (4p + 3p). Then think about which edges the cut removes and which new edges it makes.

Similar problem: a square of side 1 cm is cut from the corner of a 6 cm by 3 cm rectangle. Going round the new shape the edges are 6, 2, 1, 1, 5 and 3 cm, which add up to 18 cm, the same as the rectangle's perimeter of 2 × (6 + 3) = 18 cm.

stepByStep.text: The whole rectangle has perimeter 2 × (4p + 3p) = 14p cm.
Cutting a square from the corner removes p cm from the end of one long edge and p cm from the end of one short edge.
The cut also makes two new edges inside the corner, each p cm long. So p + p is taken away and p + p is added back.
The perimeter of the piece that is left is still 14p cm.

misconceptions.A: This takes away the two edges that were cut off. The cut also makes two new edges of the same length, so nothing is lost.
misconceptions.B: This takes away all four sides of the square. Only two edges go, and two new ones of the same length appear.
misconceptions.C: Yes! The two new inside edges exactly replace the two pieces that were cut off, so the perimeter stays 14p cm.
misconceptions.D: This adds the two new edges but does not take away the two pieces that were cut off. The changes balance out.

G5A_ALGEBRA_003.questionText: Each side of a square is s cm long, where s is a whole number greater than 3. A rectangle is made that is 3 cm longer than the square and 3 cm narrower than the square. How does the area of the rectangle compare with the area of the square?

options.text: It is always 9 sq cm smaller
It is always 6 sq cm smaller
It is always 9 sq cm bigger

hints: When a question says a rule holds for every value of a letter, try two or three values and see what stays the same.
Try s = 5. The square has area 5 × 5. The rectangle is 8 cm by 2 cm. Compare the two areas, then try another value of s.

Similar problem: a rectangle is 2 cm longer and 2 cm narrower than a square. With side 10 the areas are 100 and 12 × 8 = 96. With side 6 they are 36 and 8 × 4 = 32. Each time the rectangle is 4 sq cm smaller.

stepByStep.text: Try s = 5: the square has area 25 sq cm and the rectangle is 8 cm by 2 cm.
Try s = 10: the square has area 100 sq cm and the rectangle is 13 cm by 7 cm.
Both times the rectangle is 9 sq cm smaller: 25 − 16 = 9 and 100 − 91 = 9.
The reason: a strip 3 cm wide and s cm long is removed, but the strip added is 3 cm wide and only (s − 3) cm long, which is 3 × 3 = 9 sq cm less.
So the area of the rectangle is always 9 sq cm smaller.

misconceptions.A: The perimeter stays the same, but the area does not. Try s = 5: 25 sq cm for the square and 8 × 2 = 16 sq cm for the rectangle.
misconceptions.B: Yes! Whatever s is, the rectangle loses a 3 cm by 3 cm corner's worth of area: 9 sq cm.
misconceptions.C: The change is 3 × 3, not 3 + 3. Try s = 5 and compare 25 with 8 × 2.
misconceptions.D: The rectangle is smaller, not bigger. Try s = 5: 8 × 2 = 16 is less than 25.

G5A_ALGEBRA_004.questionText: If 2a + b = 9, what is the value of 6a + 3b − 4?
hints: You do not need to know a and b separately. Look for the given expression hiding inside the new one.
Compare 6a + 3b with 2a + b. How many times bigger is each part?
Similar problem: if x + 2y = 5, find 4x + 8y + 1. Since 4x + 8y is 4 times (x + 2y), the value is 4 × 5 + 1 = 21.

stepByStep.text: 6a is 3 times 2a, and 3b is 3 times b. So 6a + 3b is 3 times (2a + b).
Use 2a + b = 9.
Now subtract 4.
The value is 23.

misconceptions.A: 3 × 9 = 27 is the value of 6a + 3b. There is still 4 to subtract.
misconceptions.B: Here 9 was used in place of a. But 9 is the value of the whole of 2a + b, not of a alone.
misconceptions.C: Yes! 6a + 3b is three lots of 2a + b, so it is 27, and 27 − 4 = 23.
misconceptions.D: 6a + 3b is three lots of 2a + b, not two lots. Find 3 × 9 first.

G5A_ALGEBRA_005.questionText: If x − y = 4, what is the value of (x + 7) − (y − 3)?
hints: You cannot find x and y separately, so regroup the expression until x − y appears. Take care with what the minus sign does to the second bracket.
Subtracting (y − 3) means taking away y and then giving back 3, because 3 less was there to be taken away.
Similar problem: if a − b = 6, find (a + 2) − (b − 5). Taking away (b − 5) is the same as taking away b and adding 5, so the value is (a − b) + 2 + 5 = 13.

stepByStep.text: Taking away (y − 3) is the same as taking away y and then adding 3.
So the expression becomes x + 7 − y + 3, which regroups as (x − y) + 7 + 3.
Use x − y = 4.
The value is 14. You can check with x = 10 and y = 6: 17 − 3 = 14.

misconceptions.A: Yes! Taking away (y − 3) removes y and gives back 3, so the value is 4 + 7 + 3 = 14.
misconceptions.B: Here the 3 was subtracted. Try x = 10 and y = 6: (10 + 7) − (6 − 3) = 17 − 3.
misconceptions.C: The 7 and the 3 change the value too. Try x = 10 and y = 6 and work out each bracket.
misconceptions.D: 7 + 3 = 10 is part of it. The x − y part is worth 4 and needs to be included too.

G5A_ALGEBRA_006.questionText: Riya makes a row of squares with matchsticks. One square needs 4 matchsticks, two squares joined in a row need 7, and three squares need 10, because each new square shares a side with the one before it. How many squares are in the row she can make with exactly 100 matchsticks?
hints: Find how many matchsticks each extra square adds, and write a rule for n squares. Then work backwards from the total.
From 4 to 7 to 10, each new square adds 3 matchsticks. So n squares need 3 for each square plus 1 extra.
Similar problem: triangles in a row need 3, 5, 7, ... matchsticks, which is 2 for each triangle plus 1 extra. With 41 matchsticks: 41 − 1 = 40, and 40 ÷ 2 = 20 triangles.

stepByStep.text: Each new square adds 3 matchsticks, and the pattern 4, 7, 10 is always 1 more than a multiple of 3. So n squares need 3n + 1 matchsticks.
Work backwards from 100. First take away the 1 extra matchstick.
Then share the rest in threes.
Riya can make a row of 33 squares.

misconceptions.A: This uses 4 matchsticks for every square. After the first square, each new one shares a side and needs only 3.
misconceptions.B: Check with the rule: 34 squares would need 3 × 34 + 1 = 103 matchsticks, which is more than 100.
misconceptions.C: So close! This takes 4 away for the first square and shares the rest in threes, but then the first square has to be counted as well.
misconceptions.D: Yes! n squares need 3n + 1 matchsticks, and 3 × 33 + 1 = 100.

G5A_ALGEBRA_007.questionText: On day n of an experiment, plant A is (3n + 2) cm tall and plant B is (5n − 40) cm tall, where n is 10 or more. On which day is plant B taller than plant A for the first time?
hints: Plant B starts shorter but grows faster. Think about how much of the gap it closes each day.
On day 10, plant A is 32 cm and plant B is 10 cm, a gap of 22 cm. Each day A grows 3 cm and B grows 5 cm. How much does the gap shrink each day?
Similar problem: A is (2n + 10) cm and B is (4n − 6) cm. On day 8 both are 26 cm. On day 9, A is 28 cm and B is 30 cm, so B is first taller on day 9.

stepByStep.text: On day 10, plant A is 32 cm and plant B is 10 cm, so A is ahead.
Each day A grows 3 cm and B grows 5 cm, so the gap shrinks by 2 cm a day. It takes 11 days to close.
So on day 21 the plants are equal: both are 65 cm tall.
On day 22, plant A is 68 cm and plant B is 70 cm.
Plant B is taller for the first time on day 22.

misconceptions.A: On day 20, plant A is 62 cm and plant B is 60 cm, so A is still taller.
misconceptions.B: On day 21 both plants are 65 cm. They are equal, and the question asks when B is taller.
misconceptions.C: Yes! The plants are level on day 21, and on day 22 plant B is 70 cm against 68 cm.
misconceptions.D: Plant B is taller on day 42, but it has been taller for a while by then. Look for the first day.

G5A_ALGEBRA_008.questionText: Asha works out 3(n + 4) and Bala works out 3n + 4 for the same whole number n. Whatever number n is, by how much is Asha's answer greater than Bala's?
hints: Open Asha's brackets so that both expressions are written the same way, then compare them part by part.
3(n + 4) means 3 lots of n and 3 lots of 4. Write it without brackets.
Similar problem: compare 5(n + 2) with 5n + 2. Opening the brackets gives 5n + 10, which is always 10 − 2 = 8 more than 5n + 2. Check with n = 1: 15 against 7.

stepByStep.text: Open Asha's brackets: 3(n + 4) is 3n + 12.
Bala has 3n + 4. Both have 3n, so only the number parts differ.
Compare the number parts.
Asha's answer is always greater by 8. Check with n = 2: 18 against 10.

misconceptions.A: The brackets matter: in 3(n + 4) the 4 is multiplied by 3 as well. Try n = 2 and work out both.
misconceptions.B: 3 × 4 = 12 is Asha's number part. Bala's expression already has 4, so compare 12 with 4.
misconceptions.C: 4 is Bala's number part. Asha's is 3 × 4, so find the gap between the two.
misconceptions.D: Yes! 3(n + 4) is 3n + 12, which is always 8 more than 3n + 4.

G5A_ALGEBRA_009.questionText: A pen costs ₹p, where p is more than 3. Ravi buys 4 pens and gets ₹3 off his total bill. Sana buys 4 pens and gets ₹3 off the price of each pen. How many rupees more than Sana does Ravi pay?
hints: Write an expression for what each child pays. Think carefully about how many times each ₹3 is taken off.
Ravi pays 4p − 3. Sana pays 4 lots of (p − 3). Open Sana's brackets and compare.
Similar problem: 5 notebooks at ₹n each. With ₹2 off the bill you pay 5n − 2. With ₹2 off each notebook you pay 5(n − 2) = 5n − 10. The first way costs 10 − 2 = ₹8 more.

stepByStep.text: Ravi pays 4p − 3 rupees.
Sana pays 4(p − 3) rupees. Opening the brackets, this is 4p − 12.
Both have 4p, so Ravi pays more by the gap between the two savings.
Ravi pays ₹9 more than Sana.

misconceptions.A: The two deals are not the same: Sana gets ₹3 off four times, once for each pen.
misconceptions.B: Yes! Sana saves ₹12 and Ravi saves ₹3, so Ravi pays ₹9 more.
misconceptions.C: ₹3 is what Ravi saves. Sana saves ₹3 on each of her 4 pens, so compare the two savings.
misconceptions.D: ₹12 is what Sana saves in total. Ravi saves ₹3 as well, so the gap between them is smaller.

G5A_ALGEBRA_010.questionText: If p = 2q and q = 3r, which expression is equal to p + q + r?
hints: To add the three letters, first write each of them using the same letter.
q is 3r. Since p is 2 lots of q, replace q with 3r to find p in terms of r.
Similar problem: if a = 4b and b = 2c, then a = 4 × 2c = 8c, so a + b + c = 8c + 2c + c = 11c.

stepByStep.text: q is already written with r: q = 3r.
p is 2 lots of q, so p is 2 lots of 3r, which is 6r.
Add the three: 6r + 3r + r.
So p + q + r = 10r.

misconceptions.A: Yes! p is 6r and q is 3r, so p + q + r = 6r + 3r + r = 10r.
misconceptions.B: This uses p = 2r. But p is 2 lots of q, and q is 3r, so p is 6r.
misconceptions.C: 6r + 3r is right for p + q. There is one more r to add.
misconceptions.D: This adds only 2 and 3. Write p in terms of r first, and include r itself.

G5A_ALGEBRA_011.questionText: The perimeter of a rectangle is (4k + 10) cm and its length is (k + 4) cm. Which expression gives its breadth in cm?
hints: The perimeter is made of two lengths and two breadths. Work backwards from it one stage at a time.
Half of the perimeter is one length plus one breadth. Find half of 4k + 10 first.
Similar problem: perimeter (6m + 8) cm and length (2m + 3) cm. Half the perimeter is 3m + 4, and taking away the length leaves a breadth of m + 1.

stepByStep.text: Half of the perimeter is one length plus one breadth. Half of 4k + 10 is 2k + 5.
Take away the length, k + 4, from 2k + 5.
2k − k is k, and 5 − 4 is 1.
The breadth is k + 1.

misconceptions.A: This takes one length away from the whole perimeter. What is left is still one length and two breadths.
misconceptions.B: So close! Taking both lengths away leaves two breadths. Halve it to find one breadth.
misconceptions.C: This is half of the perimeter, which is one length plus one breadth. Take the length away from it.
misconceptions.D: Yes! Half the perimeter is 2k + 5, and taking away k + 4 leaves k + 1.

G5A_ALGEBRA_012.questionText: Arjun is y years old now. His father's age is 4 years more than 3 times Arjun's age. Which expression gives the sum of their ages 5 years from now?
hints: Write each person's age now, then each person's age later, and only then add.
The father's age now is 3 times y, plus 4. In 5 years, how much older will EACH of them be?
Similar problem: Diya is d years old and her mother is 2 more than 4 times her age, so 4d + 2. In 3 years they will be d + 3 and 4d + 5, and the sum will be 5d + 8.

stepByStep.text: Arjun is y now, and his father is 3y + 4.
In 5 years Arjun will be y + 5 and his father will be 3y + 4 + 5, which is 3y + 9.
Add the two ages: y + 5 + 3y + 9.
The sum of their ages will be 4y + 14.

misconceptions.A: Yes! Both of them grow 5 years older, so the sum is 4y + 4 + 10 = 4y + 14.
misconceptions.B: Here 5 years were added only once. Arjun and his father each grow 5 years older.
misconceptions.C: This is the sum of their ages now. In 5 years each of them will be 5 years older.
misconceptions.D: Arjun's own age belongs in the sum too: y for Arjun and 3y for the father part make 4y.

G5A_ALGEBRA_013.questionText: The nth term of a sequence is 6n + 5, so the first term is 11. How many terms of the sequence are less than 100?
hints: Find the last term that is still below 100, and work out which position it has in the sequence.
6n + 5 must be less than 100, so 6n must be less than 95. Find the biggest n that fits.
Similar problem: the nth term is 4n + 3. How many terms are below 50? 4n must be less than 47, so n can be at most 11 (the 11th term is 47, the 12th is 51). There are 11 terms.

stepByStep.text: For a term to be below 100, 6n + 5 must be less than 100, so 6n must be less than 95.
6 × 15 = 90 fits, but 6 × 16 = 96 is too big.
Check: the 15th term is 95 and the 16th term is 101.
So 15 terms are less than 100.

misconceptions.A: 100 ÷ 6 gives 16, but remember the + 5: the 16th term is 6 × 16 + 5 = 101, which is over 100.
misconceptions.B: Yes! The 15th term is 95 and the 16th is 101, so 15 terms are below 100.
misconceptions.C: There are 14 jumps of 6 from 11 up to 95, but the number of terms is one more than the number of jumps.
misconceptions.D: The 17th term is 6 × 17 + 5 = 107, which is well over 100. Find the last term below 100.

G5A_ALGEBRA_014.questionText: Which of these expressions gives an odd number for EVERY whole number n?
hints: An expression that works for every n must work for both odd and even values of n. Test each expression with one of each.
Try n = 1 and n = 2 in each expression. Cross out any expression that gives an even number even once.

Similar problem: which is always even, n + 2 or n × (n + 1)? With n = 1, n + 2 = 3, which is odd, so it is out. n × (n + 1) gives 2, 6, 12, 20, ... because one of two neighbouring numbers is always even.

stepByStep.text: Test n = 1 and n = 2. n + 1 gives 2 and 3, so it is not always odd. 3n gives 3 and 6, so it is not always odd.
2n + 4 gives 6 and 8. It is always even, because both parts are even.
n × (n + 1) + 1 gives 1 × 2 + 1 = 3 and 2 × 3 + 1 = 7. Both are odd.
This always happens: n and n + 1 are neighbours, so one of them is even and their product is even. Adding 1 makes it odd.
The expression that is always odd is n × (n + 1) + 1.

misconceptions.A: This is odd when n is even, but try n = 1: it gives 2.
misconceptions.B: This is odd when n is odd, but try n = 2: it gives 6.
misconceptions.C: Both 2n and 4 are even, so this is always even, never odd.
misconceptions.D: Yes! n × (n + 1) is always even, because one of two neighbouring numbers is even, and adding 1 makes it odd.

G5A_ALGEBRA_015.questionText: A taxi charges ₹40 for the first 2 km of a ride and ₹c for every km after that. Which expression gives the fare, in rupees, for a ride of d km, where d is more than 2?
hints: Split the ride into two parts: the part covered by the fixed charge and the part charged per km.
The first 2 km cost ₹40 altogether. How many km of the ride are left to be charged at ₹c each?
Similar problem: an auto charges ₹25 for the first km and ₹m for every km after that. A ride of 6 km has 6 − 1 = 5 km charged at ₹m, so the fare is 25 + m × 5. For n km it is 25 + m × (n − 1).

stepByStep.text: The first 2 km cost ₹40 in total.
That leaves (d − 2) km to be charged at ₹c each.
Those km cost c × (d − 2) rupees. The brackets show that c multiplies the whole of d − 2.
The fare is 40 + c × (d − 2).

misconceptions.A: This charges ₹c for all d km. The first 2 km are already covered by the ₹40.
misconceptions.B: Here the ₹40 is multiplied too. The ₹40 is paid only once, so it is added, not multiplied.
misconceptions.C: Yes! ₹40 covers the first 2 km and the other (d − 2) km cost ₹c each.
misconceptions.D: Without brackets, this takes away ₹2 from the fare instead of taking 2 km away from the distance.

G5A_ALGEBRA_016.questionText: A number machine takes a whole number n, doubles it, adds 6, halves the result, and then subtracts the number n that went in. What comes out?
hints: Follow the machine one action at a time with the letter n, or try two different numbers and compare what comes out.
After doubling and adding 6 the machine holds 2n + 6. Halving must be done to BOTH parts.
Similar problem: take m, multiply by 3, add 12, divide the result by 3, subtract m. That is 3m + 12, then m + 4, then 4. The machine gives 4 for every input.

stepByStep.text: Doubling n gives 2n, and adding 6 gives 2n + 6.
Halving the whole result gives n + 3, because half of 2n is n and half of 6 is 3.
Subtracting n leaves 3.
Check with n = 5: 10, 16, 8, then 8 − 5 = 3. The machine always gives 3.

misconceptions.A: Yes! Half of 2n + 6 is n + 3, and taking away n always leaves 3.
misconceptions.B: Here only the 2n was halved. The 6 is part of the result too, so it is halved as well.
misconceptions.C: This stops one action early. The machine still has to subtract n.
misconceptions.D: The 6 is halved along with the 2n, and then n is subtracted. Try n = 5 and follow each action.

G5A_ANGLES_001.questionText: At which of these times is the smaller angle between the hour hand and the minute hand of a clock exactly 45°?
hints: For each time, find where each hand points. The hour hand does not sit on a number unless the time is exactly on the hour.
At half past an hour the minute hand points at the 6 and the hour hand is halfway between two numbers. Each number-to-number gap on the clock is 30°.
A similar check at 2:30: the hour hand is halfway between the 2 and the 3, and the minute hand is on the 6. From there to the 6 is 3 and a half gaps, which is 105°.

stepByStep.text: At 4:30 the minute hand points at the 6 and the hour hand is halfway between the 4 and the 5.
From the hour hand to the 5 is half a gap, which is 15°, and from the 5 to the 6 is one gap, which is 30°.
Add the two parts.
At the other times the angles are 135°, 135° and 112.5°, so the time is 4:30.

misconceptions.A: At 1:30 the hour hand is 45° past the 12, but the minute hand is at the 6, not at the 12. Measure between the two hands.
misconceptions.B: Well done! At 4:30 the hour hand is halfway between the 4 and the 5, which is one and a half gaps from the 6: 45°.
misconceptions.C: At 10:30 the hour hand is 45° before the 12, but the minute hand is far away at the 6. Count the gaps between the hands.
misconceptions.D: The 45 here is minutes, not degrees. At 12:45 the minute hand is on the 9 and the hour hand is close to the 1.

G5A_ANGLES_002.questionText: At 12 o'clock the two hands of a clock lie exactly together. After how many minutes is the angle between them 66° for the first time?
hints: Both hands are moving, one much faster than the other. Think about how quickly the faster one pulls ahead.
In one minute the minute hand turns 6° and the hour hand turns half a degree. Find how much the gap between them grows in one minute.
A similar question: how long after 12 o'clock is the angle 33°? The gap grows by 5 and a half degrees each minute, and 6 lots of 5 and a half make 33, so it takes 6 minutes.

stepByStep.text: In one minute the minute hand turns 6° and the hour hand turns half a degree.
So the angle between them grows by 5 and a half degrees every minute, which is 11° every 2 minutes.
Find how many lots of 11° make 66°.
Six lots of 2 minutes: the angle is 66° after 12 minutes.

misconceptions.A: After 11 minutes the minute hand has turned 66°, but the hour hand has moved on a little too, so the gap is still less than 66°.
misconceptions.B: This is a little too long. Work out exactly how much the gap grows each minute: 6° less half a degree.
misconceptions.C: This uses only the hour hand's half a degree a minute. The angle between the hands grows mostly because of the minute hand.
misconceptions.D: Excellent! The gap opens by 11° every 2 minutes, so 66° takes 12 minutes.

G5A_ANGLES_003.questionText: At 10:10, what is the larger angle between the hour hand and the minute hand, measured the long way round the clock?
hints: Two things need care: where exactly the hour hand is at ten minutes past the hour, and which of the two angles is being asked for.
The minute hand points at the 2. The hour hand has moved past the 10 by 10 minutes' worth of turning, at half a degree each minute.
A similar question at 8:20: the minute hand is at the 4, which is 120° from the 12. The hour hand is at 240° + 10° = 250°. The smaller angle is 130°, so the larger one is 360° − 130° = 230°.

stepByStep.text: Measure from the 12, going clockwise. The minute hand is at the 2, which is 60°.
The hour hand is 5° past the 10.
Going clockwise from the minute hand to the hour hand is the long way round.
The other way round is only 115°, so the larger angle is 245°.

misconceptions.A: This keeps the hour hand exactly on the 10. In 10 minutes it has crept forward by 5°.
misconceptions.B: This is the smaller angle between the hands. The question asks for the angle the long way round.
misconceptions.C: Well done! The hour hand is at 305° and the minute hand at 60°, so the long way round is 245°.
misconceptions.D: This is the short way round with the hour hand left on the 10. Move the hour hand on 5° and take the long way round.

G5A_ANGLES_004.questionText: While the minute hand of a clock turns through 150°, through how many degrees does the hour hand turn?
hints: The two hands are linked by time. Find how long the minute hand takes, then ask how far the hour hand goes in that time.
The minute hand turns 360° in 60 minutes, which is 6° each minute. Find how many minutes it needs for 150°.
A similar question: while the minute hand turns 90°, 15 minutes pass. The hour hand turns 30° in 60 minutes, so in 15 minutes it turns a quarter of 30°, which is 7.5°.

stepByStep.text: The minute hand turns 6° each minute. Find the time taken.
The hour hand turns 30° in 60 minutes, which is half a degree each minute.
Find half of 25.
So the hour hand turns through 12.5°.

misconceptions.A: Well done! 150° takes 25 minutes, and at half a degree a minute the hour hand turns 12.5°.
misconceptions.B: 25 is the number of minutes that pass. The hour hand turns only half a degree in each of those minutes.
misconceptions.C: The hour hand is 12 times slower than the minute hand, not 10 times. Use the time: 25 minutes at half a degree a minute.
misconceptions.D: This divides by 60. The hour hand turns 30° in an hour, so it is 12 times slower than the minute hand.

G5A_ANGLES_005.questionText: Point O lies on a straight line AB. A ray OC is drawn from O, making the two angles AOC and COB. Ray OP cuts angle AOC into two equal parts, and ray OQ cuts angle COB into two equal parts. What is the size of angle POQ?

options.text: It changes when ray OC is moved

hints: No size is given for angle AOC, so try to see what stays the same wherever ray OC points. Testing one or two sizes of your own can help.
Angle POQ is made of half of angle AOC and half of angle COB. Think about what angle AOC and angle COB add up to.

A similar idea: angle XOZ is 120° and ray OY lies inside it. If one ray halves angle XOY and another halves angle YOZ, the angle between those two rays is half of 120°, which is 60°, wherever OY lies.

stepByStep.text: Angles AOC and COB lie side by side on a straight line, so together they make 180°.
Angle POQ is half of angle AOC together with half of angle COB.
Half of each is the same as half of the total.
So angle POQ is 90°, wherever ray OC is drawn.

misconceptions.A: The two angles change when OC moves, but one grows exactly as much as the other shrinks. Try angle AOC as 40° and then as 100° and compare.
misconceptions.B: This halves once more than needed. The two half angles together make half of 180°.
misconceptions.C: 180° is the whole straight line from A to B. Angle POQ is only the part between the two halving rays.
misconceptions.D: Lovely reasoning! Half of each angle makes half of 180°, so angle POQ is always 90°.

G5A_ANGLES_006.questionText: Two straight lines cross at a point, making four angles. Three of the four angles add up to 250°. What is the size of the smallest of the four angles?
hints: All four angles round the crossing point make a full turn. Once you know one angle, the straight lines tell you all the others.
Take 250° from 360° to find the angle that was left out of the sum. Then ask whether that angle is the smallest one.
A similar crossing: three of the four angles add up to 300°. The fourth is 60°, the angle opposite it is also 60°, and the other two are 120° each. Here the smallest angle is 60°.

stepByStep.text: Find the angle that was left out.
The angle opposite it is also 110°.
Each of the other two angles lies beside it on a straight line.
The four angles are 110°, 70°, 110° and 70°, so the smallest angle is 70°.

misconceptions.A: 110° is the angle left out of the sum, but the question asks for the smallest. Find the angle beside it on the straight line.
misconceptions.B: Well done! The fourth angle is 110°, so its neighbours are 70° each, and 70° is the smallest.
misconceptions.C: This halves 250°. The three angles in the sum are not all equal, so find the fourth angle first.
misconceptions.D: This halves the fourth angle. The angles beside 110° are found by taking it from 180°.

G5A_ANGLES_007.questionText: The supplement of an angle is 4 times its complement. What is the angle?
hints: Compare the supplement and the complement of the same angle. How far apart are they, whatever the angle is?
The supplement is what must be added to reach 180° and the complement is what must be added to reach 90°, so the supplement is 90° more than the complement.
A similar puzzle: the supplement of an angle is 3 times its complement. The extra 90° is then 2 times the complement, so the complement is 45° and the angle is 45°.

stepByStep.text: For any angle, the supplement is 90° more than the complement.
Here the supplement is 4 times the complement, so the extra 90° is 3 times the complement.
Find the complement.
Take the complement from 90°: the angle is 60°.

misconceptions.A: 30° is the complement of the angle. Take it from 90° to get the angle itself.
misconceptions.B: Excellent! The complement is 30° and the supplement is 120°, which is 4 times as much, so the angle is 60°.
misconceptions.C: This comes from sharing 90° into 5 parts. The supplement and the complement do not add up to 90°; they differ by 90°.
misconceptions.D: This comes from sharing 180° into 5 parts. The supplement and the complement do not add up to 180°; they differ by 90°.

G5A_ANGLES_008.questionText: The complement and the supplement of an angle add up to 194°. What is the angle?
hints: Think about how the complement and the supplement are each made from the angle, and how many times the angle is taken away in all.
The complement is 90° less the angle and the supplement is 180° less the angle. Together they are 270° less two copies of the angle.
A similar puzzle: the complement and supplement of an angle add up to 210°. Then 270° − 210° = 60° is two copies of the angle, so the angle is 30°. Check: 60° + 150° = 210°.

stepByStep.text: The complement is 90° less the angle, and the supplement is 180° less the angle.
Together they are 270° less two copies of the angle. Find the two copies.
Halve it to find the angle.
Check: 52° + 142° = 194°, so the angle is 38°.

misconceptions.A: 76° is two copies of the angle, because the angle is taken away in the complement and again in the supplement. Halve it.
misconceptions.B: This takes 180° from 194°. Write the complement and the supplement each in terms of the angle, then add them.
misconceptions.C: This is the complement of the angle. The question asks for the angle itself.
misconceptions.D: Well done! Two copies of the angle make 76°, so the angle is 38°, and 52° + 142° = 194°.

G5A_ANGLES_009.questionText: Angle P and angle Q are complementary. Angle Q and angle R are supplementary. How much bigger is angle R than angle P?

options.text: It depends on the size of angle Q

hints: No sizes are given, so try a size of your own for angle Q, work out P and R, and then try another size. Compare the results.
Angle P is what must be added to Q to make 90°. Angle R is what must be added to the same Q to make 180°.
A similar idea with other totals: A and B add up to 50, and B and C add up to 80. Whatever B is, C is 30 more than A, because 80 is 30 more than 50.

stepByStep.text: Angle P and angle Q add up to 90°, so P is 90° less Q.
Angle Q and angle R add up to 180°, so R is 180° less Q.
The same Q is taken away both times, so the difference is the difference of the totals.
So angle R is always 90° bigger than angle P.

misconceptions.A: Lovely reasoning! The same angle Q is taken from 180° and from 90°, so R is always 90° more than P.
misconceptions.B: The sizes of P and R do change with Q, but they change together. Try Q as 30° and then as 50° and compare R − P each time.
misconceptions.C: Try an example: if Q is 40°, then P is 50° and R is 140°. Look at how far apart P and R are.
misconceptions.D: 180° is what Q and R add up to. The question asks how much bigger R is than P.

G5A_ANGLES_010.questionText: Two angles are complementary. Measured in whole degrees, one of them is a multiple of 7 and the other is a multiple of 11. What is the difference between the two angles?
hints: There are only a few multiples of 11 below 90. Test them in order and see what each one leaves.
Start with 11°: the other angle would be 79°. Is 79 a multiple of 7? Carry on with 22°, 33° and so on.

A similar search: two supplementary angles, one a multiple of 50 and the other a multiple of 30. Testing 50°, 100° and 150° leaves 130°, 80° and 30°. Only the last is a multiple of 30, so the angles are 150° and 30° and they differ by 120°.

stepByStep.text: Complementary angles add up to 90°. The multiples of 11 below 90 are 11, 22, 33, 44, 55, 66, 77 and 88.
Taking each from 90 leaves 79, 68, 57, 46, 35, 24, 13 and 2.
Only 35 is a multiple of 7, so the angles are 55° and 35°.
Subtract: the difference is 20°.

misconceptions.A: 56° and 33° are a multiple of 7 and a multiple of 11, but they add up to 89°, one short of 90°. Keep testing.
misconceptions.B: 42° and 44° fit the multiples, but they add up to only 86°. Complementary angles must make exactly 90°.
misconceptions.C: Well searched! Only 55° and 35° fit, and their difference is 20°.
misconceptions.D: 77° and 11° add up to 88°, not 90°. Test each multiple of 11 and check what is left from 90°.

G5A_ANGLES_011.questionText: Two straight roads run exactly east to west and are parallel, one to the north of the other. Bela stands at point B on the north road and Dev stands at point D on the south road. A lamp post E stands between the two roads, to the east of both children. The straight line from B to E makes an angle of 35° with the north road, and the straight line from D to E makes an angle of 40° with the south road. What is the size of angle BED, the angle at the lamp post between the two lines?
hints: Sketch the two roads and the bend at E. The angle at E touches neither road, so think about adding a helpful line of your own.
Draw a line through E parallel to the two roads. It cuts angle BED into two parts. Compare the top part with the 35° angle at B.
A similar bend: with angles of 20° at the top road and 50° at the bottom road, a parallel line through the bend makes alternate angles of 20° and 50°, so the angle at the bend is 20° + 50° = 70°.

stepByStep.text: Draw a line through E that is parallel to both roads. It splits angle BED into an upper part and a lower part.
The upper part and the 35° angle at B are alternate angles between parallel lines, so the upper part is 35°.
In the same way the lower part equals the 40° angle at D.
Add the two parts: angle BED is 75°.

misconceptions.A: Well done! A parallel line through E gives alternate angles of 35° and 40°, which add up to 75°.
misconceptions.B: Taking the total from 180° is for two angles on the same side between parallel lines. Here each given angle is equal to one part of angle BED.
misconceptions.C: The two parts of the angle at E lie side by side, one above the helping line and one below it, so they are added, not subtracted.
misconceptions.D: This uses only the angle at B. The line from D also plays a part, so split angle BED with a line parallel to the roads.

G5A_ANGLES_012.questionText: A straight line crosses two parallel lines. An angle at the first crossing and its alternate angle at the second crossing add up to 124°. What is the size of each obtuse angle formed at the crossings?
hints: Recall what is special about alternate angles between parallel lines, then read again which angles the question asks for.
Alternate angles between parallel lines are equal, so share 124° equally between the two. Are those angles obtuse?
A similar crossing: two alternate angles add up to 100°, so each is 50°. The obtuse angles beside them on the straight line are 180° − 50° = 130°.

stepByStep.text: Alternate angles between parallel lines are equal.
Find each of the two alternate angles.
62° is acute. Each obtuse angle lies beside a 62° angle on a straight line.
Take it from 180°: each obtuse angle is 118°.

misconceptions.A: 62° is each of the alternate angles, and it is acute. The obtuse angles lie beside them on the straight line.
misconceptions.B: This takes 124° from 180°, but 124° is the total of two equal angles, not one angle. Halve it first.
misconceptions.C: Well done! Each alternate angle is 62°, so the obtuse angles beside them are 118°.
misconceptions.D: 124° is the total of the two alternate angles together, not the size of one angle at a crossing.

G5A_ANGLES_013.questionText: Two parallel lines are drawn, one above the other. P is a point on the top line. Q and R are points on the bottom line, with Q to the left of R. The line PQ makes an angle of 50° with the top line on the left of P, and the line PR makes an angle of 62° with the top line on the right of P. What is the largest angle of triangle PQR?
hints: Sketch it. Three angles sit side by side at P along the top line, and the two given ones also reappear somewhere in the triangle.
At P, the 50° angle, the angle QPR and the 62° angle together make the straight top line. Find angle QPR first.

A similar picture with 40° on the left and 60° on the right: the angle at the top point is 180° − 40° − 60° = 80°, and the base angles are 40° and 60° by alternate angles, so the largest angle is 80°.

stepByStep.text: The three angles at P lie along a straight line. Find angle QPR.
Angle PQR and the 50° angle are alternate angles between the parallel lines, so angle PQR is 50°.
In the same way angle PRQ is 62°.
The triangle has angles 68°, 50° and 62°, so its largest angle is 68°.

misconceptions.A: 62° is one of the base angles of the triangle. Work out the angle at P as well before choosing the largest.
misconceptions.B: Well done! The angle at P is 68° and the base angles are 50° and 62°, so 68° is the largest.
misconceptions.C: This adds the two given angles. Together with angle QPR they make the 180° of the straight top line.
misconceptions.D: This is the angle between PQ and the top line on the other side of PQ. It reaches outside the triangle.

G5A_ANGLES_014.questionText: Ravi turns 135° clockwise and then 270° anticlockwise. He is now facing North. In which direction was he facing at the start?
hints: North is where Ravi finishes, not where he begins. Think about how to undo a turn.
The two turns together are the same as one turn of 135° anticlockwise. To go back to the start, make the opposite turn from North.
A similar puzzle: Tina turns 90° clockwise and then 45° anticlockwise and ends facing East. Her turns together are 45° clockwise, so she started 45° anticlockwise of East, which is North-East.

stepByStep.text: A turn of 135° clockwise followed by 270° anticlockwise is the same as one turn of 135° anticlockwise.
To find the start, undo this from North: turn 135° clockwise.
From North, 90° clockwise is East and 45° more is South-East.
Check: from South-East, 135° clockwise is West, and 270° anticlockwise from West is North. So he started facing South-East.

misconceptions.A: This makes the two turns starting from North. North is where Ravi ends, so the turns have to be undone.
misconceptions.B: Check it: from North-East, 135° clockwise is South, and 270° anticlockwise from South is West, not North.
misconceptions.C: Check it: from North-West, 135° clockwise is East, and 270° anticlockwise from East is South, not North.
misconceptions.D: Well done! Undoing a net turn of 135° anticlockwise from North leads back to South-East.

G5A_ANGLES_015.questionText: Asha faces North-East. She turns through 3 right angles clockwise and then through 135° anticlockwise. What is the smallest turn that will make her face North-East again?
hints: Find the direction Asha faces after her two turns. From there she can turn back either way round, so compare the two ways.
Three right angles are 270°. From North-East, 270° clockwise is North-West. Now make the 135° anticlockwise turn from North-West.

A similar puzzle: Ravi faces East, turns 180° clockwise and then 45° anticlockwise, so he faces South-West. To face East again he can turn 225° clockwise or 135° anticlockwise, and the smaller is 135° anticlockwise.

stepByStep.text: Three right angles are 270°. From North-East, 270° clockwise is North-West.
From North-West, 135° anticlockwise is South. So Asha now faces South.
From South to North-East is 225° going clockwise through West and North, or 135° going anticlockwise through South-East and East.
The smaller of the two is 135° anticlockwise.

misconceptions.A: This turn does reach North-East, but it goes the long way round. Try turning the other way and compare the sizes.
misconceptions.B: Her two turns together were 135° clockwise. Turning the same way again takes her further from North-East; undo it by turning the other way.
misconceptions.C: Well done! Asha ends facing South, and the short way back to North-East is 135° anticlockwise.
misconceptions.D: From South, 225° anticlockwise ends at North-West. Find where she is facing first, then count the turn to North-East each way.

G5A_ANGLES_016.questionText: A toy robot faces North. Each time a bell rings it turns 135° clockwise. After how many rings does it face North again for the first time?
hints: Facing North again means the robot has turned through an exact number of full turns, not just a bit more than one.
Add up the turning after each ring: 135°, 270°, 405° and so on. Look for the first total that is a multiple of 360°.
A similar robot turns 150° at each ring. Its totals are 150°, 300°, 450° and so on, and the first total that is a whole number of full turns is 1800°, which is 5 full turns, reached after 12 rings.

stepByStep.text: The robot faces North again when its total turning is a whole number of full turns of 360°.
The first of these that is a multiple of 360° is 1080°, which is 3 full turns.
So the robot faces North again after 8 rings.

misconceptions.A: Well done! 8 turns of 135° make 1080°, exactly 3 full turns, and no smaller number of turns gives whole turns.
misconceptions.B: After 3 rings the robot has turned 405°, which is 45° more than a full turn, so it faces North-East.
misconceptions.C: After 4 rings the robot has turned 540°, which is one and a half turns, so it faces South.
misconceptions.D: After 6 rings the robot has turned 810°, which is 90° more than two full turns, so it faces East.

G5A_ANGLES_017.questionText: Four rays OA, OB, OC and OD start from the same point O. Going round in order, angle AOB is 20°, angle BOC is 30° and angle COD is 40°. Counting every angle that has two of these four rays as its arms, how many of the angles are acute?
hints: An angle can be made by any two of the rays, not only by rays that are next to each other. List the pairs of rays in an orderly way.
Besides the three given angles there are angle AOC, angle BOD and angle AOD. Find each by adding the parts it is made of.
A similar picture: rays OP, OQ and OR with angle POQ 50° and angle QOR 60°. The angles are 50°, 60° and the combined angle POR of 110°. Two of the three are acute.

stepByStep.text: The three given angles are 20°, 30° and 40°, and all three are acute.
Angle AOC is 20° + 30° = 50° and angle BOD is 30° + 40° = 70°. Both are acute.
Angle AOD is made of all three parts.
Angle AOD is a right angle, not an acute angle. So the acute angles are 20°, 30°, 40°, 50° and 70°, which makes 5.

misconceptions.A: These are only the three angles that are given. Rays that are not next to each other also make angles, such as angle AOC.
misconceptions.B: Six is the number of angles in all. Check the largest one, angle AOD: an angle of exactly 90° is a right angle, not an acute angle.
misconceptions.C: One angle is missing. List them by pairs of rays: AOB, AOC, AOD, BOC, BOD and COD.
misconceptions.D: Well counted! The angles are 20°, 30°, 40°, 50°, 70° and 90°, and all but the right angle are acute: 5.

G5A_ANGLES_018.questionText: Two angles are supplementary. Which of these statements is true for every such pair of angles?

options.text: One of them must be obtuse
The larger one is always more than 90°

hints: A statement is true for every pair only if no pair at all breaks it. Hunt for an unusual pair that might break each statement.
Try the pair 90° and 90°. They add up to 180°, so they are supplementary. Test each statement on this pair.
A similar test: for two complementary angles, is it always true that one is bigger than 45°? Trying 45° and 45° shows it is not, since they add up to 90° and neither is bigger than 45°.

stepByStep.text: Supplementary angles add up to 180°. One special pair is 90° and 90°.
In that pair neither angle is obtuse, the two are equal, and neither is more than 90°, so three of the statements are not always true.
Two acute angles are each less than 90°, so together they are less than 180° and can never be supplementary.
So the statement that is always true is: they cannot both be acute.

misconceptions.A: This is true for most pairs, but think of 90° and 90°: they are supplementary and neither is obtuse.
misconceptions.B: Well reasoned! Two angles that are each less than 90° add up to less than 180°, so they cannot both be acute.
misconceptions.C: Two right angles are equal and add up to 180°, so supplementary angles can be equal.
misconceptions.D: In the pair 90° and 90° there is no angle bigger than 90°, so this is not true for every pair.

G5A_ANGLES_019.questionText: Angle AOB is 70° and angle BOC is 50°. The two angles share the arm OB. Which answer gives every possible size of angle AOC?
hints: No picture is given, so ask yourself whether there is more than one way to draw it. Where can ray OC go?
Draw angle AOB first. Ray OC makes 50° with OB, and it can be drawn on either side of OB. Sketch both pictures.
A similar case: angle XOY is 80° and angle YOZ is 30°, sharing the arm OY. If OZ is on the far side of OY, angle XOZ is 110°. If OZ is on the same side as OX, it is 50°. So it can be 50° or 110°.

stepByStep.text: Ray OC makes an angle of 50° with OB, and it can lie on either side of OB.
If OC is on the other side of OB from OA, the two angles lie side by side and are added.
If OC is on the same side of OB as OA, the angles overlap and are subtracted.
So angle AOC can be 20° or 120°.

misconceptions.A: 120° is right when OC lies on the far side of OB. There is another place where OC can be drawn: on the same side as OA.
misconceptions.B: Well done! OC can be drawn on either side of OB, which gives 70° + 50° = 120° or 70° − 50° = 20°.
misconceptions.C: 20° is right when OC lies between OA and OB. OC can also be drawn on the other side of OB.
misconceptions.D: 120° is one possible size. For the other, the two angles overlap, so take 50° from 70°.

G5A_ANGLES_020.questionText: A wheel has 9 spokes, equally spaced and numbered 1 to 9 in order round the wheel. What is the smaller angle between spoke 2 and spoke 8?
hints: On a wheel you can go from one spoke to another in two directions. Find the angle of one gap first, then compare the two ways round.
Nine equal gaps make a full turn of 360°, so find the angle between two neighbouring spokes. Then count the gaps from spoke 2 to spoke 8 each way.
A similar wheel has 8 spokes, so each gap is 45°. From spoke 1 to spoke 7 is 6 gaps one way, which is 270°, but only 2 gaps the other way, through spoke 8. The smaller angle is 90°.

stepByStep.text: Find the angle between neighbouring spokes.
Counting up from spoke 2 to spoke 8 there are 6 gaps, which is 240°.
Going the other way, from spoke 8 to spoke 9, then 1, then 2, there are only 3 gaps.
Three gaps of 40°: the smaller angle is 120°.

misconceptions.A: 240° is the angle the long way round, through spokes 3 to 7. The wheel is a circle, so try going the other way.
misconceptions.B: This counts 7 gaps. From spoke 2 to spoke 8 there are 6 gaps, and the short way round has even fewer.
misconceptions.C: This comes from counting 7 gaps one way. Count gaps, not spokes: there are 6 one way and 3 the other way.
misconceptions.D: Well done! Each gap is 40°, and the short way round has 3 gaps, so the smaller angle is 120°.

G5A_BODMAS_001.questionText: The value of 72 ÷ 6 + 3 × 4 − 2 is 22. One pair of brackets is put in so that the value becomes 30. Around which part do the brackets go?
hints: Brackets change which operation is done first. Test each placement, always using the correct order of operations.
Try the brackets round 6 + 3. The expression becomes 72 ÷ 9 × 4 − 2. Work it out, doing division and multiplication from left to right.
A similar one: 40 ÷ 4 + 4 × 2 is 10 + 8 = 18. With brackets round 4 + 4 it becomes 40 ÷ 8 × 2 = 5 × 2 = 10.

stepByStep.text: Brackets are done first, so test each placement with the correct order. Start with brackets round 6 + 3.
Division and multiplication are done from left to right.
Then subtract.
Check the tempting placement round 4 − 2: multiplication still comes before addition, so it gives 18, not 30.
So the brackets go round (6 + 3).

misconceptions.A: This seems to give 30 if you work from left to right. But multiplication comes before addition, so it is 12 + 3 × 2 = 12 + 6 = 18. Try the brackets round the addition instead.
misconceptions.B: Yes! With these brackets it is 72 ÷ 9 × 4 − 2. Then 72 ÷ 9 = 8, 8 × 4 = 32 and 32 − 2 = 30.
misconceptions.C: Multiplication is already done before adding and subtracting, so these brackets change nothing and the value stays 22. Look for brackets that change the order.
misconceptions.D: Inside these brackets 3 × 4 is done first, so the bracket is 18, and 72 ÷ 18 − 2 = 2. Try bracketing only the addition.

G5A_BODMAS_002.questionText: The signs +, − and × are put into the three boxes, each sign used exactly once: 8 □ 2 □ 5 □ 3. What is the greatest value the expression can have?
hints: There are only six ways to place the three signs. Think about which pair of numbers gains most from × and which number is best to take away.
Put × in each of the three boxes in turn. For each one, choose the better place for + and −, remembering that × is done first.
A similar one: with + and × in 6 □ 3 □ 4, the choices are 6 + 3 × 4 = 6 + 12 = 18 and 6 × 3 + 4 = 18 + 4 = 22, so the greatest value is 22.

stepByStep.text: With × in the first box, the better choice is 8 × 2 + 5 − 3.
With × in the middle box, the better choice is 8 + 2 × 5 − 3.
With × in the last box, the better choice is 8 − 2 + 5 × 3, which takes away only the small 2.
Comparing 18, 15 and 21, the greatest value is 21.

misconceptions.A: This is 8 × 2 + 5 − 3. Multiplying the first two numbers looks strong, but try the × between 5 and 3 and compare.
misconceptions.B: This comes from 8 + 2 × 5 − 3 worked from left to right. Multiplication must be done first, so that expression is really 8 + 10 − 3 = 15. Test the other arrangements with the correct order.
misconceptions.C: This is 8 + 2 × 5 − 3. It is a correct value, but another arrangement is greater. Try each place for the × sign.
misconceptions.D: Well done! 8 − 2 + 5 × 3 = 8 − 2 + 15 = 21, and no other arrangement of the three signs gives more.

hints: Start from the innermost bracket and move outwards. Inside any bracket, the usual order still applies.
Inside the round brackets do 2 × 2 first, then subtract from 7. Use that value in the curly bracket next.
A similar one: 30 − [12 − {8 − (5 − 1 × 2)}]. Round brackets: 5 − 2 = 3. Curly: 8 − 3 = 5. Square: 12 − 5 = 7. So 30 − 7 = 23.

stepByStep.text: Round brackets first, multiplying before subtracting.
Curly brackets next.
Square brackets next.
Now the front part, division and multiplication from left to right.
Subtract the bracket: the value is 27.

misconceptions.A: Lovely work! The brackets give 7 − 4 = 3, then 9 − 3 = 6, then 15 − 6 = 9, and 72 ÷ 6 × 3 = 36, so 36 − 9 = 27.
misconceptions.B: This comes from doing 7 − 2 first inside the round brackets. Multiplication comes first there: 2 × 2 = 4, then 7 − 4 = 3.
misconceptions.C: This comes from 36 − 15 − 6. The whole square bracket is taken away, and its value is 15 − 6 = 9, so it is 36 − 9.
misconceptions.D: This comes from working 15 − 9 − 3 inside the square bracket. The curly bracket must be finished first: 9 − 3 = 6, then 15 − 6 = 9.

G5A_BODMAS_004.questionText: The digits 2, 3 and 4 are written in the three boxes, each digit used once: 24 ÷ □ + 6 × □ − □. What is the greatest value the expression can have?
hints: Each box does a different job. Ask how much the value changes when a bigger or a smaller digit goes into each box.
The digit that multiplies 6 should clearly be the largest, 4. Now compare the two ways to place 2 and 3 in the other boxes.
A similar one: digits 1, 2, 5 in 30 ÷ □ + 2 × □ − □. Try 30 ÷ 1 + 2 × 5 − 2 = 30 + 10 − 2 = 38 and 30 ÷ 2 + 2 × 5 − 1 = 15 + 10 − 1 = 24. The first is greater.

stepByStep.text: The largest digit, 4, should multiply 6, because each extra 1 there adds 6.
Now place 2 and 3. Dividing by 2 and taking away 3:
Dividing by 3 and taking away 2:
The other arrangements are smaller still, so the greatest value is 33.

misconceptions.A: This is 24 ÷ 3 + 6 × 4 − 2. Taking away the smallest digit feels right, but compare what happens when 24 is divided by 2 instead of 3.
misconceptions.B: This comes from working 24 ÷ 2 + 6 × 4 − 3 from left to right. Do the division and the multiplication first, then add and subtract.
misconceptions.C: Great thinking! 24 ÷ 2 + 6 × 4 − 3 = 12 + 24 − 3 = 33. Dividing by the smallest digit is worth more than taking away the smallest digit.
misconceptions.D: This is 24 ÷ 2 + 6 × 3 − 4, the digits in the order given. Try giving the largest digit to the multiplication.

G5A_BODMAS_005.questionText: Which number goes in the box to make this true? 6 + 4 × (□ − 3) ÷ 2 = 20
hints: Work backwards. Decide which operation is done last on the left side and undo that one first.
The 6 is added last, so the part 4 × (□ − 3) ÷ 2 must equal 20 − 6. Carry on undoing from there.
A similar one: 5 + 3 × (□ − 2) ÷ 3 = 9. The multiplication part must be 4. Then 3 × (□ − 2) = 12, so □ − 2 = 4 and the box is 6.

stepByStep.text: The 6 is added last, so undo it first.
So 4 × (□ − 3) ÷ 2 = 14. Undo the division by 2.
So 4 × (□ − 3) = 28. Undo the multiplication by 4.
The bracket equals 7, so add 3 back. The number in the box is 10.

misconceptions.A: This comes from adding 6 + 4 first. The 4 belongs to the multiplication, so the 6 is added last. Check: 6 + 4 × 4 ÷ 2 = 6 + 8 = 14, not 20.
misconceptions.B: This makes 4 × (□ − 3) ÷ 2 equal to 20 by itself. Remember the 6 that is added: that part must equal 14.
misconceptions.D: The bracket (□ − 3) must equal 7. To find the box, add 3 back to 7 rather than taking 3 away.

G5A_BODMAS_006.questionText: Exactly one of these statements is true. Which one?
hints: Work out the left side of every statement with the correct order of operations, not simply from left to right.
In each statement, find the ÷ and × parts and do those first. Then add and subtract from left to right and compare with the number after the equals sign.
A similar check: is 20 − 8 ÷ 4 + 1 = 4 true? Division first: 8 ÷ 4 = 2. Then 20 − 2 + 1 = 19, so that statement is not true.

stepByStep.text: First statement: divide first.
Second statement: multiply first.
Fourth statement: both multiplications first.
Third statement: divide, then multiply, then subtract.
So the true statement is 30 − 12 ÷ 2 × 3 = 12.

misconceptions.A: Yes! Division and multiplication come first, from left to right: 12 ÷ 2 = 6 and 6 × 3 = 18. Then 30 − 18 = 12.
misconceptions.B: This gives 7 only if 18 − 6 is done first. Division comes first: 6 ÷ 3 = 2, so the value is 18 − 2 + 3 = 19.
misconceptions.C: This gives 30 only if 4 + 6 is done first. Multiplication comes first: 6 × 5 = 30, so the value is 4 + 30 − 20 = 14.
misconceptions.D: This gives 30 only if you work straight from left to right. Both multiplications come first: 18 − 6 = 12.

G5A_BODMAS_007.questionText: Meena says, 'Putting brackets round the last two numbers of an expression never changes its value.' For which of these expressions does the value change when brackets are put round its last two numbers?
hints: Work out each expression twice: once as written, with the correct order, and once with brackets round the last two numbers.
Start with 20 − 6 + 4. As written it is 14 + 4. With brackets it is 20 − (6 + 4). Compare the two values.
A similar pair: 15 − 5 + 2 = 12, but 15 − (5 + 2) = 15 − 7 = 8. The bracket after the minus sign changed the value.

stepByStep.text: 20 + 6 − 4 and 20 + (6 − 4) are both 22, and 20 × 6 ÷ 3 and 20 × (6 ÷ 3) are both 40.
In 20 + 6 × 4 the multiplication is done first anyway, so both forms give 44.
As written, 20 − 6 + 4 is worked from left to right.
With brackets the whole of 6 + 4 is taken away.
So the value changes for 20 − 6 + 4.

misconceptions.A: Without brackets the multiplication is already done first: 20 + 24 = 44. The brackets round 6 × 4 give 44 too. Look for a minus sign in front of the bracket.
misconceptions.B: 20 + 6 − 4 = 22 and 20 + (6 − 4) = 22. Adding a bracket changes nothing here. Try the expression that subtracts first.
misconceptions.C: 20 × 6 ÷ 3 = 40 and 20 × (6 ÷ 3) = 40. Multiplying by a bracket changes nothing here. Try the expression that subtracts first.
misconceptions.D: Well spotted! 20 − 6 + 4 = 18, but 20 − (6 + 4) = 10. A minus sign in front of a bracket takes away everything inside it.

G5A_BODMAS_008.questionText: Kabir worked out 40 − 8 × □ + 6 from left to right, without using the order of operations, and got 134. What is the correct value of the expression, with the same number in the box?
hints: First find the number in the box by following Kabir's left-to-right working backwards. Then start again with the correct order.
From left to right Kabir did 40 − 8 = 32, then 32 × □, then added 6 to reach 134. Undo the + 6 and then the × 32.
A similar one: someone works 30 − 5 × □ + 2 from left to right and gets 77. Then 25 × □ = 75, so the box is 3. The correct value is 30 − 15 + 2 = 17.

stepByStep.text: Kabir's first step was 40 − 8 = 32, so his working was 32 × □ + 6 = 134. Undo the + 6.
Undo the multiplication by 32. The number in the box is 4.
Now use the correct order: multiply first.
Then subtract and add from left to right. The correct value is 14.

misconceptions.A: 4 is the number in the box. The question asks for the value of the whole expression, so now work out 40 − 8 × 4 + 6 with the correct order.
misconceptions.B: Super! Kabir's way gives 32 × □ + 6 = 134, so the box holds 4. With the correct order, 40 − 8 × 4 + 6 = 40 − 32 + 6 = 14.
misconceptions.C: This comes from 40 − 32 − 6. Only 32 is taken away. The 6 is added: 40 − 32 + 6.
misconceptions.D: 128 is what 32 × □ equals in Kabir's working. Use it to find the box, then work out the expression with the correct order.

G5A_BODMAS_009.questionText: Which of these expressions has the greatest value? Try to decide by reasoning, without multiplying 999 by 12.
hints: Three of the expressions contain 999 × 12 or something close to it. Compare what is added to it or taken from it in each one.
In 999 × 12 + 12 ÷ 12, decide which operation is done before the addition. What is being added to 999 × 12?
A similar one: which is greater, 50 × 8 + 8 ÷ 8 or 50 × 8 − 8? The first is 400 + 1 = 401 and the second is 400 − 8 = 392, so the first is greater.

stepByStep.text: 999 × (12 − 12) + 12 has a bracket equal to 0, so it is only 12.
In 999 × 12 + 12 ÷ 12 the division is done before the addition, so it is 1 more than 999 × 12.
So the greatest is 999 × 12 + 12 ÷ 12.

misconceptions.A: This is 999 × 12 with 12 taken away, so it is less than 999 × 12. Look for an expression that adds something to 999 × 12.
misconceptions.B: Excellent reasoning! 12 ÷ 12 is done before the addition, so this is 999 × 12 plus 1, a little more than 999 × 12.
misconceptions.C: Multiplying by 12 and then dividing by 12 brings you back to 999 + 12 = 1011, far less than 999 × 12.
misconceptions.D: The bracket is 0, and 999 × 0 = 0, so this expression is only 12.

G5A_BODMAS_010.questionText: In 24 □ 8 □ 2 □ 5 = 25, each box holds one of the signs +, −, × and ÷, and no sign is used twice. There is only one way to make the statement true. Which sign is not used?
hints: 25 is just a little more than 24. Think about how the other three numbers could together add only 1.
Try 24 − 8 ÷ 2 first, remembering that the division is done before the subtraction. Then see which sign and number finish the job.
A similar one: 20 □ 6 □ 3 □ 4 = 22. Try 20 − 6 ÷ 3 + 4: the division gives 2, then 20 − 2 + 4 = 22. The sign not used there is ×.

stepByStep.text: 25 is 1 more than 24, so the numbers 8, 2 and 5 must together add 1.
Dividing first, 8 ÷ 2 = 4, and taking 4 away and adding 5 adds exactly 1.
Check the tempting arrangement 24 ÷ 8 + 2 × 5 with the correct order: it is 13, not 25.
The signs used are −, ÷ and +, so the sign not used is the multiplication sign ×.

misconceptions.A: This comes from 24 ÷ 8 + 2 × 5 worked from left to right. With the correct order it is 3 + 10 = 13, not 25. Try starting with 24 and taking a little away.
misconceptions.B: Without + the choices are made from −, × and ÷, and none of those arrangements gives 25. Try 24 − 8 ÷ 2 and see what is still needed.
misconceptions.C: Without ÷ the choices are made from +, − and ×, and none of those arrangements gives 25. Try dividing 8 by 2 first.
misconceptions.D: Yes! 24 − 8 ÷ 2 + 5 = 24 − 4 + 5 = 25, so the sign left out is the multiplication sign ×.

G5A_DECIMALS_001.questionText: Anu copied a decimal number that had one digit after the decimal point, but she left out the decimal point. The number she wrote was 40.5 more than the real number. What was the real number?
hints: Leaving out the decimal point of a number with one decimal digit makes it a certain number of times bigger. How many times?
The number she wrote is 10 times the real number. So the extra 40.5 is 9 times the real number.
Similar problem: a number with one decimal digit loses its point and becomes 21.6 more. The extra is 9 times the real number, so the real number is 21.6 ÷ 9 = 2.4, and 24 − 2.4 = 21.6.

stepByStep.text: Without its decimal point, a number with one decimal digit becomes 10 times as big.
So the number she wrote is 10 times the real number, and the difference is 9 times the real number.
9 times the real number is 40.5.
Check: 45 − 4.5 = 40.5. The real number was 4.5.

misconceptions.A: This divides 40.5 by 10. The number she wrote is 10 times the real one, so the difference between them is 9 times the real number.
misconceptions.B: Yes! 45 is 40.5 more than 4.5, so the real number was 4.5.
misconceptions.C: 45 is the number Anu wrote, without the decimal point. The real number is one-tenth of it.
misconceptions.D: 0.45 has two digits after the point, and 45 − 0.45 is not 40.5. Try dividing 40.5 by 9.

G5A_DECIMALS_002.questionText: A train journey takes 2.4 hours. The train leaves at 9:50 a.m. At what time does it arrive?
hints: A decimal part of an hour is not a number of minutes. Change it into minutes first.
0.4 of an hour is 4 tenths of 60 minutes. Work that out before adding to the starting time.
Similar problem: a film lasts 1.5 hours and starts at 3:45 p.m. 0.5 of an hour is 30 minutes, so the film lasts 1 hour 30 minutes and ends at 5:15 p.m.

stepByStep.text: 0.4 of an hour is 4 tenths of 60 minutes, which is 24 minutes.
So the journey takes 2 hours 24 minutes.
2 hours after 9:50 a.m. is 11:50 a.m.
Now add 24 minutes: 10 minutes reach 12:00 noon, and the other 14 minutes make 12:14 p.m. The train arrives at 12:14 p.m.

misconceptions.A: This reads 2.4 hours as 2 hours 40 minutes. 0.4 of an hour is 4 tenths of 60 minutes, which is 24 minutes.
misconceptions.B: This reads 2.4 hours as 2 hours 4 minutes. 0.4 of an hour is 24 minutes.
misconceptions.C: Yes! 2.4 hours is 2 hours 24 minutes, and 9:50 a.m. plus that is 12:14 p.m.
misconceptions.D: The journey time of 2 hours 24 minutes is right, but it was added to 10:00 a.m. instead of 9:50 a.m.

G5A_DECIMALS_003.questionText: A pencil costs ₹4.50 and an eraser costs ₹2.50. Anu buys 12 items, some pencils and some erasers, and pays exactly ₹44. How many pencils does she buy?
hints: Imagine all 12 items were erasers, then swap erasers for pencils one at a time and watch the bill grow.
12 erasers would cost 12 × ₹2.50 = ₹30. Each swap of an eraser for a pencil adds ₹2 to the bill.
Similar problem: pens cost ₹6 and clips cost ₹1, and 10 items cost ₹25. Ten clips cost ₹10. Each swap to a pen adds ₹5, and ₹15 more is needed, so there are 3 pens.

stepByStep.text: If all 12 items were erasers, the bill would be ₹30.
The real bill is ₹14 more.
Each pencil in place of an eraser adds ₹2.
So the number of pencils is 7.
Check: 7 pencils cost ₹31.50 and 5 erasers cost ₹12.50, which is ₹44 for 12 items. She buys 7 pencils.

misconceptions.A: 5 is the number of erasers. The question asks for the pencils.
misconceptions.B: 6 pencils and 6 erasers cost ₹27 + ₹15 = ₹42, which is ₹2 too little. Swap one more eraser for a pencil.
misconceptions.C: 8 pencils and 4 erasers cost ₹36 + ₹10 = ₹46, which is ₹2 too much.
misconceptions.D: Yes! 7 pencils and 5 erasers cost ₹31.50 + ₹12.50 = ₹44.

G5A_DECIMALS_004.questionText: Dividing any number by 0.25 always gives the same result as:
hints: Think of 0.25 as a fraction, and ask how many of them fit into 1.
0.25 is one quarter. How many quarters are there in 1 whole? In 2 wholes?
Similar problem: dividing by 0.5 asks how many halves fit. There are 2 halves in every whole, so dividing by 0.5 is the same as multiplying by 2. For example, 3 ÷ 0.5 = 6.

stepByStep.text: 0.25 is one quarter.
Dividing by one quarter asks how many quarters fit into the number, and each whole holds 4 quarters.
Test with 3: there are 12 quarters in 3.
So dividing by 0.25 is the same as multiplying the number by 4.

misconceptions.A: Yes! Each whole holds 4 quarters, so dividing by 0.25 multiplies the number by 4.
misconceptions.B: 0.25 is one quarter, but dividing BY a quarter is not the same as taking a quarter. Test with 1 ÷ 0.25: four quarters fit into 1, so the result is bigger, not smaller.
misconceptions.C: The digits 2 and 5 appear in 0.25, but 0.25 is one quarter, not 25. Test with 1 ÷ 0.25, which is 4.
misconceptions.D: Dividing by 25 would make the number much smaller. Dividing by 0.25, a number less than 1, makes it bigger.

G5A_DECIMALS_005.questionText: The sum of two decimal numbers is 7.2 and their difference is 1.8. What is the larger of the two numbers?
hints: If the two numbers were equal, each would be half of the sum. The difference tells you how to adjust.
Add the difference to the sum: 7.2 + 1.8. This gives twice the larger number. Can you see why?
Similar problem: two numbers add up to 5.0 and differ by 1.4. Twice the larger is 5.0 + 1.4 = 6.4, so the larger is 3.2 and the smaller is 1.8.

stepByStep.text: Adding the difference to the sum gives two copies of the larger number.
Twice the larger number is 9.
So the larger number is 4.5.
Check: the smaller is 2.7, and 4.5 + 2.7 = 7.2 while 4.5 − 2.7 = 1.8. The larger number is 4.5.

misconceptions.A: This takes the difference away from the sum. That gives 5.4, which is twice the smaller number and not one of the two numbers.
misconceptions.B: Yes! 4.5 and 2.7 add up to 7.2 and are 1.8 apart.
misconceptions.C: 3.6 is half of the sum. The numbers are not equal: they are 1.8 apart.
misconceptions.D: 2.7 is the smaller of the two numbers. The question asks for the larger.

G5A_DECIMALS_006.questionText: How many numbers with exactly two digits after the decimal point, such as 3.47, are greater than 3.4 and less than 3.5?
hints: Write both end numbers with two digits after the point, then list what lies strictly between them.
3.4 is the same as 3.40 and 3.5 is the same as 3.50. Which hundredths come after 3.40 and before 3.50?
Similar problem: between 6.2 and 6.25, the numbers with two decimal digits are 6.21, 6.22, 6.23 and 6.24. The ends 6.20 and 6.25 are not counted, so there are 4 numbers.

stepByStep.text: Write the ends with two decimal digits: 3.4 = 3.40 and 3.5 = 3.50.
The numbers strictly between them are 3.41, 3.42, 3.43, 3.44, 3.45, 3.46, 3.47, 3.48 and 3.49.
3.40 and 3.50 are not counted, because they are equal to the ends.
There are 9 such numbers.

misconceptions.A: It may seem that nothing lies between 3.4 and 3.5, but hundredths do: 3.41 is greater than 3.4 and less than 3.5.
misconceptions.B: This takes 50 − 40 = 10. That count includes one of the ends, 3.40 or 3.50, which are equal to 3.4 and 3.5 and not between them.
misconceptions.C: Yes! The numbers are 3.41 up to 3.49, which is 9 numbers.
misconceptions.D: This counts 3.40 and 3.50 as well. They are equal to 3.4 and 3.5, so they are not between them.

G5A_DECIMALS_007.questionText: In the number 4.75, what is the place value of the digit 7?
hints: Name the places to the right of the decimal point in order.
The first place after the decimal point is the tenths place. Which digit sits there in 4.75?
Similar problem: in 6.38 the digit 3 is in the first place after the point, so its value is 3 tenths.

stepByStep.text: In 4.75, the digit 4 is in the ones place.
The first digit after the decimal point is in the tenths place, and that digit is 7.
The place value of the digit 7 is 7 tenths.

misconceptions.A: The ones place is just before the decimal point, where the 4 is. The 7 comes just after the point.
misconceptions.B: The hundredths place is the second place after the point, where the 5 is.
misconceptions.C: The tens place is two places before the decimal point. The 7 is after the point.
misconceptions.D: Yes! The 7 is in the first place after the decimal point, so it is 7 tenths.

G5A_DECIMALS_008.questionText: Which digit is in the hundredths place in 36.482?
hints: The places after the decimal point are tenths, hundredths and thousandths, in that order.
Count two places to the right of the decimal point in 36.482.
Similar problem: in 5.917 the places after the point are 9 tenths, 1 hundredth and 7 thousandths, so the hundredths digit is 1.

stepByStep.text: After the decimal point in 36.482 come 4 tenths, 8 hundredths and 2 thousandths.
The hundredths place is the second place after the point.
The digit in the hundredths place is 8.

misconceptions.A: Yes! The second digit after the decimal point is 8, and that is the hundredths place.
misconceptions.B: 4 is in the tenths place, the first place after the point. The hundredths place is the second.
misconceptions.C: 2 is in the thousandths place, the third place after the point.
misconceptions.D: 3 is in the tens place, before the decimal point. Hundredths come after the point.

G5A_DECIMALS_009.questionText: Which of these numbers is the greatest: 3.4, 3.9, 3.1 or 3.7?
hints: Compare the whole-number parts first, then the tenths.
All four numbers have 3 ones, so look at the digit after the decimal point.
Similar problem: among 5.2, 5.8, 5.5 and 5.6, the ones are all 5 and the biggest tenths digit is 8, so 5.8 is the greatest.

stepByStep.text: All four numbers have 3 in the ones place.
The tenths digits are 4, 9, 1 and 7. The biggest is 9.
The greatest number is 3.9.

misconceptions.A: 3.4 has 4 tenths. One of the other numbers has more tenths.
misconceptions.B: Yes! 9 tenths is the most, so 3.9 is the greatest.
misconceptions.C: 3.1 has only 1 tenth, so it is the smallest of the four.
misconceptions.D: 3.7 has 7 tenths, which is a lot, but one number has even more.

G5A_DECIMALS_010.questionText: Which of these numbers is the smallest: 0.52, 0.35, 0.25 or 0.55?
hints: Compare the tenths digits first. If two are the same, compare the hundredths.
The tenths digits are 5, 3, 2 and 5. Which is the smallest?
Similar problem: among 0.61, 0.48, 0.73 and 0.84, the smallest tenths digit is 4, so 0.48 is the smallest.

stepByStep.text: All four numbers have 0 ones, so compare the tenths digits: 5, 3, 2 and 5.
The smallest tenths digit is 2, in 0.25.
The smallest number is 0.25.

misconceptions.A: 0.52 has 5 tenths. Look for a number with fewer tenths.
misconceptions.B: 0.35 has 3 tenths, but one number has only 2 tenths.
misconceptions.C: Yes! 0.25 has only 2 tenths, the fewest of the four.
misconceptions.D: 0.55 has 5 tenths and 5 hundredths, so it is the greatest of the four, not the smallest.

hints: Line up the decimal points, then add tenths with tenths and ones with ones.
Add the tenths first: 5 tenths and 3 tenths.
Similar problem: 4.2 + 3.6. Tenths: 2 + 6 = 8. Ones: 4 + 3 = 7. The sum is 7.8.

stepByStep.text: Add the tenths: 5 tenths and 3 tenths make 8 tenths.
Add the ones.
Put them together: 3 ones and 8 tenths make 3.8.

misconceptions.A: The ones add up to 3, but 5 tenths and 3 tenths make 8 tenths, not 2 tenths.
misconceptions.B: The tenths are right, but the ones are 2 + 1 = 3.
misconceptions.C: This takes 1.3 away from 2.5. The question asks for the sum.
misconceptions.D: Yes! 3 ones and 8 tenths make 3.8.

G5A_DECIMALS_012.questionText: Rani had ₹8.50. She spent ₹3.20 on a pencil. How much money does she have left?
hints: Money left means taking away what was spent.
Line up the decimal points and subtract: paise from paise, rupees from rupees.
Similar problem: ₹7.90 − ₹2.40. Paise: 90 − 40 = 50. Rupees: 7 − 2 = 5. The answer is ₹5.50.

stepByStep.text: Subtract the paise: 30 paise are left.
Subtract the rupees: 5 rupees are left.
Rani has ₹5.30 left.

misconceptions.A: Yes! 5 rupees and 30 paise are left, which is ₹5.30.
misconceptions.B: This adds the two amounts. Rani spent money, so take ₹3.20 away from ₹8.50.
misconceptions.C: The rupees are right, but the paise are 50 − 20 = 30, not 70.
misconceptions.D: The paise are right, but the rupees are 8 − 3 = 5.

hints: Multiplying by 10 makes each digit worth ten times as much, so the decimal point moves.
Move the decimal point in 4.6 one place to the right.
Similar problem: 7.3 × 10. Moving the point one place to the right gives 73.

stepByStep.text: Multiplying by 10 moves the decimal point one place to the right.
4.6 becomes 46.

misconceptions.A: This is 4.6 × 100. Multiplying by 10 moves the point only one place.
misconceptions.B: Yes! The point moves one place to the right, so 4.6 becomes 46.
misconceptions.C: This is 4.6 ÷ 10. Multiplying makes the number bigger, so the point moves to the right.
misconceptions.D: Multiplying by 10 moves the decimal point; it does not put a zero in the middle. 4.6 × 10 is 46.

hints: Multiplying by 100 makes each digit worth a hundred times as much, so the decimal point moves.
Move the decimal point in 3.25 two places to the right.
Similar problem: 1.47 × 100. Moving the point two places to the right gives 147.

stepByStep.text: Multiplying by 100 moves the decimal point two places to the right.
3.25 becomes 325.

misconceptions.A: This is 3.25 × 10. For × 100 the point moves two places.
misconceptions.B: This is 3.25 × 1000. For × 100 the point moves only two places.
misconceptions.C: Yes! The point moves two places to the right, so 3.25 becomes 325.
misconceptions.D: Here only the 3 was multiplied by 100. Every digit moves two places, giving 325.

hints: Dividing by 10 makes each digit worth one-tenth as much, so the decimal point moves.
Think of 57 as 57.0 and move the point one place to the left.
Similar problem: 83 ÷ 10. Moving the point one place to the left gives 8.3.

stepByStep.text: Dividing by 10 moves the decimal point one place to the left. 57 is the same as 57.0.
57 becomes 5.7.

misconceptions.A: This is 57 × 10. Dividing makes the number smaller.
misconceptions.B: This is 57 ÷ 100. Dividing by 10 moves the point only one place.
misconceptions.C: Dividing by 10 does not put a zero between the digits. 57 ÷ 10 is 5 ones and 7 tenths.
misconceptions.D: Yes! The point moves one place to the left, so 57 becomes 5.7.

G5A_DECIMALS_016.questionText: How is 'seven tenths' written as a decimal?
hints: Tenths go in the first place after the decimal point.
There are no ones, so write 0 before the point, then put the 7 in the tenths place.
Similar problem: three tenths is written 0.3, with the 3 in the first place after the point.

stepByStep.text: Seven tenths means 7 parts out of 10 equal parts of one whole.
There are no ones, so write 0, then the decimal point, then 7 in the tenths place.
Seven tenths is written 0.7.

misconceptions.A: Yes! The 7 goes in the first place after the point: 0.7.
misconceptions.B: 0.07 is seven hundredths. Tenths go in the first place after the point.
misconceptions.C: 7 is seven ones. Seven tenths is less than one whole.
misconceptions.D: 70 is seven tens. Tenths are parts of one whole, so the number is less than 1.

G5A_DIVISIBILITY_001.questionText: The 5-digit number 4P27Q is divisible by both 5 and 9, where P and Q each stand for a digit. How many different numbers fit?
hints: Use one rule to list the choices for one digit, then use the other rule to find the other digit for each choice.
A number divisible by 5 ends in 0 or 5, so Q has two possible values. Take them one at a time and use the rule for 9.
Similar problem: 6PQ is divisible by 5 and 9. If Q = 0 the digits add up to 6 + P, so P = 3. If Q = 5 they add up to 11 + P, so P = 7. That gives 2 numbers: 630 and 675.

stepByStep.text: Divisible by 5 means Q is 0 or 5.
If Q = 0, the digits add up to 4 + P + 2 + 7 + 0 = 13 + P. For a multiple of 9, P must be 5, giving 45,270.
If Q = 5, the digits add up to 18 + P. This is a multiple of 9 when P = 0 or P = 9, giving 40,275 and 49,275.
So there are 3 numbers that fit.

misconceptions.A: This is the count when Q is 0. A number divisible by 5 can also end in 5, so check that case too.
misconceptions.B: Nearly there! When Q = 5 the digits add up to 18 + P, and P = 0 works as well as P = 9.
misconceptions.C: Yes! The numbers are 45,270, 40,275 and 49,275.
misconceptions.D: Check each one with the rule for 9: the digits must add up to a multiple of 9. Only three numbers pass both rules.

G5A_DIVISIBILITY_002.questionText: The 3-digit number 4P8 is divisible by 6 but NOT by 9, where P stands for a digit. How many different digits can P be?
hints: There are two conditions. Find every digit that fits the first one, then check each of them against the second.
4P8 is even whatever P is, so for divisibility by 6 you only need the digits to add up to a multiple of 3. The digits add up to 12 + P.

Similar problem: 5P4 is divisible by 6 but not by 9. The digits add up to 9 + P, so P can be 0, 3, 6 or 9 for a multiple of 3. P = 0 and P = 9 make a multiple of 9, so they are out. That leaves 2 digits: 3 and 6.

stepByStep.text: 4P8 ends in 8, so it is always even. It is divisible by 6 when its digits add up to a multiple of 3.
The digits add up to 12 + P, which is a multiple of 3 when P is 0, 3, 6 or 9.
The number must NOT be divisible by 9. With P = 6 the digits add up to 18, a multiple of 9, so 6 is out.
That leaves P = 0, 3 or 9, so P can be 3 different digits.

misconceptions.A: These are the digits that make 4P8 divisible by 6. One of them also makes it divisible by 9, which the question does not allow.
misconceptions.B: This counts the digit that makes 4P8 divisible by 9. The question asks for the digits where it is NOT divisible by 9.
misconceptions.C: P = 0 counts too: 408 is divisible by 6 and its digits add up to 12, which is not a multiple of 9.
misconceptions.D: Yes! P can be 0, 3 or 9. P = 6 is left out because 468 is divisible by 9.

G5A_DIVISIBILITY_003.questionText: How many whole numbers from 1 to 50 have exactly three factors?
hints: Factors usually come in pairs, which gives an even number of them. Think about what kind of number has an odd number of factors.
Square numbers have an odd number of factors, because one factor pairs with itself. List the squares up to 50 and count the factors of each.
Similar problem: which numbers from 51 to 200 have exactly three factors? They must be squares of primes: 11 × 11 = 121 and 13 × 13 = 169. So there are 2.

stepByStep.text: Factors come in pairs, so a number has an odd number of factors only when it is a square: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49.
