misconceptions.C: The 1 comes at the start of each block of 6, at positions 1, 7, 13 and so on up to 97. The 100th number is three places after that.
misconceptions.D: Yes! The block 1, 2, 3, 4, 3, 2 repeats every 6 numbers, and the 100th number is the 4th in its block.

G5A_SEQUENCES_004.questionText: A sequence starts 100, 93, 86, 79, … and goes down by 7 each time. How many terms of the sequence are greater than 0?
hints: Work out how many times 7 can be taken away before the terms drop below 0. Then think about how steps and terms are related.
100 ÷ 7 is 14 remainder 2. So after 14 steps down the term is 2. Is that term still greater than 0? And how many terms are there if 14 steps have been taken?
Similar problem: 50, 44, 38, … going down by 6. 50 ÷ 6 is 8 remainder 2, so after 8 steps the term is 2. Counting the first term as well, there are 8 + 1 = 9 terms greater than 0.

stepByStep.text: See how many 7s can be taken from 100.
So after 14 steps down, the term is 2, which is still greater than 0. One more step would give a number below 0.
The terms are the starting term and then one term for each step.
So 15 terms are greater than 0.

misconceptions.A: 14 is the number of steps down from 100 to 2. The first term, 100, counts as a term too.
misconceptions.B: Yes! There are 14 steps from 100 down to 2, which makes 15 terms.
misconceptions.C: The 16th term would be 2 − 7, which is below 0, so it does not count.
misconceptions.D: Check by dividing: 100 ÷ 7 is 14 remainder 2, so 14 steps can be taken, and the first term counts as well.

hints: Working from left to right would take very long. Look for small groups of neighbouring terms that are easy to work out.
Put brackets round the terms two at a time: (100 − 99) + (98 − 97) + … What is each bracket worth?
Similar problem: 20 − 19 + 18 − 17 + … + 2 − 1. Each pair such as (20 − 19) is worth 1. There are 20 numbers, so 10 pairs, and the value is 10.

stepByStep.text: Each pair is worth 1.
There are 100 numbers, so there are 50 pairs.
Add up the pairs.
The value is 50.

misconceptions.A: There are 100 numbers, but each pair uses two of them. Count the pairs.
misconceptions.B: The terms do not cancel out: each pair such as 100 − 99 leaves 1 behind.
misconceptions.C: Yes! There are 50 pairs and each is worth 1.
misconceptions.D: So close! Count the pairs again: 100 numbers make exactly 50 pairs, and the last pair (2 − 1) counts too.

G5A_SEQUENCES_006.questionText: In the sequence 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 4, 4, 4, 4, …, each whole number n is written n times. What is the 50th term?
hints: Work out the position where each number is written for the last time. The running total of 1 + 2 + 3 + … helps.
The last 1 is at position 1, the last 2 at position 1 + 2 = 3, the last 3 at position 1 + 2 + 3 = 6. Keep adding until the total passes 50.
Similar problem: the 20th term. 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 = 15, so the last 5 is at position 15. The next six positions, 16 to 21, hold 6s. So the 20th term is 6.

stepByStep.text: Add 1 + 2 + 3 + … to find where each number ends. The 9s end at position 45.
The next ten terms are all 10s. They end at position 55.
Position 50 lies between 46 and 55.
So the 50th term is 10.

misconceptions.A: Yes! The 9s end at position 45, and positions 46 to 55 all hold 10.
misconceptions.B: The last 9 is at position 45. The 50th term comes after that, among the next group of numbers.
misconceptions.C: The 11s only start at position 56. Position 50 comes before that.
misconceptions.D: The 7s end at position 28, which is well before position 50. Keep adding to the running total.

G5A_SEQUENCES_007.questionText: A sequence starts with 7. The rule is: if a term is odd, add 5 to get the next term; if a term is even, halve it to get the next term. So the sequence begins 7, 12, 6, 3, … What is the 50th term?
hints: Keep applying the rule until you see a group of terms coming round again. Note exactly where the repeating part begins.
Carry on from 3: it is odd, so add 5 to get 8. Then 4, then 2, then 1. What comes after 1, and have you seen that number before?

Similar problem: start with 5; if odd add 3, if even halve. The sequence is 5, 8, 4, 2, 1, 4, 2, 1, … The block 4, 2, 1 repeats from the 3rd term. For the 21st term, 21 − 2 = 19 terms lie in the repeating part, and 19 ÷ 3 leaves remainder 1, so it is the 1st number of the block, which is 4.

stepByStep.text: Continue the sequence: 7, 12, 6, 3, 8, 4, 2, 1, 6, 3, 8, 4, 2, 1, … The block 6, 3, 8, 4, 2, 1 repeats, starting from the 3rd term.
The first two terms are not in the repeating part, so set them aside.
The block has 6 numbers. See how many whole blocks fit into 48 terms.
Exactly 8 whole blocks fit, so the 50th term is the last number of a block.
The last number of the block 6, 3, 8, 4, 2, 1 is 1, so the 50th term is 1.

misconceptions.A: This counts the repeating block from the very first term. The block 6, 3, 8, 4, 2, 1 only starts at the 3rd term, after 7 and 12.
misconceptions.B: 6 starts each block, at the 3rd, 9th, 15th terms and so on up to the 51st. The 50th term is just before a new block starts.
misconceptions.C: 8 is the 3rd number of each block. The 50th term is the 48th term of the repeating part, which is the end of a block.
misconceptions.D: Yes! After 7 and 12, the block 6, 3, 8, 4, 2, 1 repeats, and the 50th term is the last number of the 8th block.

G5A_SPEED_001.questionText: Asha cycles at a steady speed of 12 km/hr. How far does she cycle in 3 hours?
hints: Speed tells you how far something goes in one hour. Distance is speed multiplied by time.
Asha goes 12 km in the first hour, 12 km in the second and 12 km in the third.
A similar one: a cyclist going 10 km/hr for 2 hours covers 10 × 2 = 20 km.

stepByStep.text: Distance is speed multiplied by time.
Multiply 12 km/hr by 3 hours.
Asha cycles 36 km.

misconceptions.A: This adds 12 and 3. She covers 12 km in each of the 3 hours, so multiply.
misconceptions.B: Great job! She covers 12 km in every hour, so in 3 hours she covers 12 × 3 = 36 km.
misconceptions.C: This divides 12 by 3. She covers 12 km in each of the 3 hours, so multiply.
misconceptions.D: This subtracts 3 from 12. She covers 12 km in each of the 3 hours, so multiply.

G5A_SPEED_002.questionText: A snail crawls 5 cm every minute. How far does it crawl in 8 minutes?
hints: The snail covers the same distance every minute. Distance is speed multiplied by time.
The speed is 5 cm each minute and the time is 8 minutes. Multiply them.
A similar one: an ant that walks 4 cm every minute walks 4 × 6 = 24 cm in 6 minutes.

stepByStep.text: Distance is speed multiplied by time.
Multiply 5 cm each minute by 8 minutes.
The snail crawls 40 cm.

misconceptions.A: This adds 5 and 8. The snail crawls 5 cm in each of the 8 minutes, so multiply.
misconceptions.B: This subtracts 5 from 8. The snail crawls 5 cm in each of the 8 minutes, so multiply.
misconceptions.C: This is 5 cm for 9 minutes. The snail crawls for 8 minutes.
misconceptions.D: You got it! The snail crawls 5 cm in each minute, so in 8 minutes it crawls 5 × 8 = 40 cm.

G5A_SPEED_003.questionText: Ravi swims at a steady speed of 2 metres every second. How long does he take to swim 50 metres?
hints: Time is distance divided by speed.
Ask how many lots of 2 metres fit into 50 metres. Each lot takes 1 second.
A similar one: a swimmer who covers 2 metres every second swims 30 metres in 30 ÷ 2 = 15 seconds.

stepByStep.text: Time is distance divided by speed.
Divide 50 metres by 2 metres each second.
Ravi takes 25 seconds.

misconceptions.A: Well done! Every second takes him 2 metres further, so 50 metres takes 50 ÷ 2 = 25 seconds.
misconceptions.B: This multiplies 50 by 2. To find the time, divide the distance by the speed.
misconceptions.C: This adds 50 and 2. To find the time, divide the distance by the speed.
misconceptions.D: This subtracts 2 from 50. To find the time, divide the distance by the speed.

G5A_SPEED_004.questionText: Rahul walks at a steady speed of 4 km/hr. How long does he take to walk 12 km?
hints: Time is distance divided by speed.
Ask how many lots of 4 km fit into 12 km. Each lot takes 1 hour.
A similar one: walking at 5 km/hr, a walk of 10 km takes 10 ÷ 5 = 2 hours.

stepByStep.text: Time is distance divided by speed.
Divide 12 km by 4 km/hr.
Rahul takes 3 hours.

misconceptions.A: This multiplies 12 by 4. To find the time, divide the distance by the speed.
misconceptions.B: This adds 12 and 4. To find the time, divide the distance by the speed.
misconceptions.C: Excellent thinking! He covers 4 km in each hour, so 12 km takes 12 ÷ 4 = 3 hours.
misconceptions.D: This subtracts 4 from 12. To find the time, divide the distance by the speed.

G5A_SPEED_005.questionText: A boat travels 45 km along a river in 3 hours at a steady speed. What is the speed of the boat?
hints: Speed is the distance covered in one unit of time. Speed is distance divided by time.
The boat covers 45 km in 3 hours. Share 45 km equally among the 3 hours.
A similar one: a boat that travels 40 km in 4 hours has a speed of 40 ÷ 4 = 10 km/hr.

stepByStep.text: Speed is distance divided by time.
Divide 45 km by 3 hours.
The speed of the boat is 15 km/hr.

misconceptions.A: This multiplies 45 by 3. Speed is the distance covered in one hour, so divide the distance by the time.
misconceptions.B: This adds 45 and 3. Speed is the distance covered in one hour, so divide the distance by the time.
misconceptions.C: Great job! The boat covers 45 km in 3 equal hours, so in one hour it covers 45 ÷ 3 = 15 km.
misconceptions.D: This subtracts 3 from 45. Speed is the distance covered in one hour, so divide the distance by the time.

G5A_SPEED_006.questionText: A horse gallops 600 metres in 2 minutes at a steady speed. How many metres does it gallop in one minute?
hints: The distance covered in one minute is the speed. Speed is distance divided by time.
The horse covers 600 metres in 2 minutes. Share 600 metres equally between the 2 minutes.
A similar one: a horse that gallops 800 metres in 2 minutes covers 800 ÷ 2 = 400 metres in one minute.

stepByStep.text: Speed is distance divided by time.
Divide 600 metres by 2 minutes.
The horse gallops 300 metres in one minute.

misconceptions.A: You got it! The horse covers 600 metres in 2 equal minutes, so in one minute it covers 600 ÷ 2 = 300 metres.
misconceptions.B: This multiplies 600 by 2. One minute is half of the time, so the distance is half as well.
misconceptions.C: This adds 600 and 2. Share the 600 metres equally between the 2 minutes.
misconceptions.D: This subtracts 2 from 600. Share the 600 metres equally between the 2 minutes.

G5A_SPEED_007.questionText: A toy car moves 10 cm every second. How long does it take to move 80 cm?
hints: Time is distance divided by speed.
Ask how many lots of 10 cm fit into 80 cm. Each lot takes 1 second.
A similar one: a toy car that moves 10 cm every second takes 60 ÷ 10 = 6 seconds to move 60 cm.

stepByStep.text: Time is distance divided by speed.
Divide 80 cm by 10 cm each second.
The toy car takes 8 seconds.

misconceptions.A: This multiplies 80 by 10. To find the time, divide the distance by the speed.
misconceptions.B: This adds 80 and 10. To find the time, divide the distance by the speed.
misconceptions.C: This subtracts 10 from 80. To find the time, divide the distance by the speed.
misconceptions.D: Well done! Every second takes the car 10 cm further, so 80 cm takes 80 ÷ 10 = 8 seconds.

G5A_SPEED_008.questionText: Kavya walks 100 metres in 50 seconds at a steady speed. What is her speed in metres per second?
hints: Speed is the distance covered in one unit of time. Speed is distance divided by time.
Kavya covers 100 metres in 50 seconds. Share 100 metres equally among the 50 seconds.
A similar one: someone who walks 90 metres in 30 seconds has a speed of 90 ÷ 30 = 3 metres per second.

stepByStep.text: Speed is distance divided by time.
Divide 100 metres by 50 seconds.
Kavya's speed is 2 metres per second.

misconceptions.A: This multiplies 100 by 50. Speed is the distance covered in one second, so divide the distance by the time.
misconceptions.B: Excellent thinking! She covers 100 metres in 50 equal seconds, so in one second she covers 100 ÷ 50 = 2 metres.
misconceptions.C: This adds 100 and 50. Speed is the distance covered in one second, so divide the distance by the time.
misconceptions.D: This subtracts 50 from 100. Speed is the distance covered in one second, so divide the distance by the time.

G5A_SPEED_009.questionText: A lorry travels at a steady speed of 40 km/hr for 5 hours. What distance does it cover?
hints: Speed tells you how far something goes in one hour. Distance is speed multiplied by time.
The lorry goes 40 km in every one of the 5 hours. Multiply 40 by 5.
A similar one: a lorry going 30 km/hr for 4 hours covers 30 × 4 = 120 km.

stepByStep.text: Distance is speed multiplied by time.
Multiply 40 km/hr by 5 hours.
The lorry covers 200 km.

misconceptions.A: This adds 40 and 5. The lorry covers 40 km in each of the 5 hours, so multiply.
misconceptions.B: Great job! The lorry covers 40 km in every hour, so in 5 hours it covers 40 × 5 = 200 km.
misconceptions.C: This divides 40 by 5. The lorry covers 40 km in each of the 5 hours, so multiply.
misconceptions.D: This subtracts 5 from 40. The lorry covers 40 km in each of the 5 hours, so multiply.

G5A_SPEED_010.questionText: Four friends each cycled for exactly 1 hour. Ravi covered 14 km, Sana covered 11 km, Tina covered 16 km and Uday covered 9 km. Who cycled at the greatest speed?
hints: When everyone travels for the same time, the fastest is the one who goes the furthest.
Each friend cycled for 1 hour, so the distance each one covered is also the speed in km/hr. Compare the four distances.
A similar one: in 1 hour Meena walks 5 km and Arjun walks 4 km. Meena covers more in the same time, so Meena is faster.

stepByStep.text: All four cycled for the same time, 1 hour, so compare the distances.
The distances are 14 km, 11 km, 16 km and 9 km. The greatest is 16 km.
So Tina cycled at the greatest speed.

misconceptions.A: Ravi covered 14 km in the hour. Look for the friend who covered the greatest distance in the same time.
misconceptions.B: Sana covered 11 km in the hour. Look for the friend who covered the greatest distance in the same time.
misconceptions.C: Uday covered 9 km, the shortest distance, so he was the slowest. Look for the greatest distance.
misconceptions.D: Yes! In the same time, the one who goes furthest is the fastest. Tina covered 16 km, more than anyone else.

G5A_TRIANGLES_001.questionText: How many of these five sets of lengths can be the three sides of a triangle? Set 1: 3 cm, 4 cm, 7 cm. Set 2: 5 cm, 5 cm, 9 cm. Set 3: 2 cm, 6 cm, 9 cm. Set 4: 4 cm, 7 cm, 10 cm. Set 5: 6 cm, 6 cm, 12 cm.
hints: Imagine fixing the longest stick on the table and hinging the two shorter sticks at its ends. When can their tips meet above it?
For each set, add the two shorter lengths and compare the total with the longest length. Think hard about the sets where they are exactly equal.
A similar check: 2 cm, 3 cm, 5 cm cannot make a triangle, because 2 + 3 is exactly 5 and the short sticks lie flat on the long one. But 3 cm, 3 cm, 5 cm can, because 3 + 3 is more than 5.

stepByStep.text: Three lengths make a triangle only when the two shorter ones together are more than the longest.
Set 1: 3 + 4 = 7, only equal, so no. Set 2: 5 + 5 = 10, more than 9, so yes. Set 3: 2 + 6 = 8, less than 9, so no.
Set 4: 4 + 7 = 11, more than 10, so yes. Set 5: 6 + 6 = 12, only equal, so no.
Only Set 2 and Set 4 make triangles, so the answer is 2.

misconceptions.A: Well done! Only 5, 5, 9 and 4, 7, 10 have two shorter sides that together beat the longest, so the answer is 2.
misconceptions.B: This also counts Set 1 and Set 5. There the two shorter sides exactly equal the longest, so they would lie flat along it with no room to rise.
misconceptions.C: One of the sets counted here only just misses. Check Set 1 and Set 5 again: equal is not enough.
misconceptions.D: There is one more. Check Set 2 and Set 4 again by adding the two shorter sides.

G5A_TRIANGLES_002.questionText: Mira has five sticks of lengths 2 cm, 3 cm, 4 cm, 5 cm and 7 cm. She picks three sticks at a time and tries to make a triangle with them as its sides. How many different triangles can she make?
hints: Not every choice of three sticks will close up into a triangle. List the choices in an orderly way so that none is missed, and test each one.
Start with the choices that use the 2 cm stick: 2, 3, 4 and 2, 3, 5 and 2, 3, 7 and so on. For each, compare the two shorter sticks together with the longest.
A similar task with sticks of 1 cm, 2 cm, 3 cm and 4 cm: the choices are 1, 2, 3 and 1, 2, 4 and 1, 3, 4 and 2, 3, 4. Only 2, 3, 4 works, because 2 + 3 is more than 4, so just 1 triangle can be made.

stepByStep.text: There are 10 ways to choose three of the five sticks. A choice makes a triangle only if the two shorter sticks together are longer than the longest.
With the 2 cm stick: 2, 3, 4 works and 2, 4, 5 works. But 2, 3, 5 and 2, 5, 7 are only equal, and 2, 3, 7 and 2, 4, 7 are too short.
Without the 2 cm stick: 3, 4, 5 and 3, 5, 7 and 4, 5, 7 work, but 3, 4, 7 is only equal.
So Mira can make 5 triangles.

misconceptions.A: Ten is the number of ways to choose three sticks, but some choices cannot close up. Try 2, 3 and 7: the short sticks cannot reach each other.
misconceptions.B: This counts choices such as 2, 3, 5 where the two short sticks exactly equal the long one. Those lie flat and make no triangle.
misconceptions.C: Well done! The choices that work are 2, 3, 4 and 2, 4, 5 and 3, 4, 5 and 3, 5, 7 and 4, 5, 7: that is 5.
misconceptions.D: One is missing. Go through the choices in order, starting with those that use the 2 cm stick.

G5A_TRIANGLES_003.questionText: Two sides of a triangle are 4 cm and 9 cm long. The third side is a whole number of centimetres. How many different lengths can the third side have?
hints: The third side cannot be too long or too short. Find both limits, then count the whole numbers strictly between them.
If the third side is the longest, it must be less than 4 + 9. If 9 cm is the longest, then 4 plus the third side must be more than 9.
A similar triangle has sides 3 cm and 8 cm. The third side must be more than 5 cm and less than 11 cm, so it can be 6, 7, 8, 9 or 10 cm: that is 5 different lengths.

stepByStep.text: The third side must be shorter than the other two together.
With 4 cm it must beat the 9 cm side, so it must be longer than their difference.
So the third side is more than 5 cm and less than 13 cm: it can be 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11 or 12 cm.
Counting these gives 7 different lengths.

misconceptions.A: Well done! The third side can be any whole number from 6 cm to 12 cm, which is 7 lengths.
misconceptions.B: This includes 5 cm and 13 cm. With those lengths the sides lie flat in a straight line, so no triangle is formed.
misconceptions.C: 12 cm is the longest the third side can be. The question asks how many different lengths are possible.
misconceptions.D: This subtracts 6 from 12. When counting from 6 to 12, both ends are included, so list them and count.

G5A_TRIANGLES_004.questionText: Three villages P, Q and R do not lie in one straight line. Straight roads join each pair of villages. Road PQ is 7 km long and road QR is 12 km long. Which of these could be the length of road PR?
hints: The three roads form a triangle. Think about going from P to R directly, and going from P to R by way of Q.
The direct road PR must be shorter than going round through Q, which is 7 km + 12 km. It also cannot be too short: 7 km and PR together must be more than 12 km.
A similar map: road AB is 6 km and road BC is 10 km, with the three villages not in a line. Road AC must be more than 4 km and less than 16 km, so 15 km is possible but 16 km and 4 km are not.

stepByStep.text: The direct road must be shorter than the way round through Q.
Roads PQ and PR together must be longer than road QR, so PR is longer than the difference.
So PR is more than 5 km and less than 19 km. Exactly 19 km or exactly 5 km would put the villages in a straight line.
Of the lengths offered, only 18 km fits.

misconceptions.A: 19 km is the length of the way round through Q. The direct road would be that long only if Q lay on the straight line from P to R.
misconceptions.B: With PR equal to 5 km, roads PQ and PR together would be exactly 12 km, so P would lie on the straight road from Q to R.
misconceptions.C: Well done! PR must lie between 5 km and 19 km without touching either, and 18 km fits.
misconceptions.D: With PR equal to 4 km, roads PQ and PR together are only 11 km, too short to reach the 12 km between Q and R.

G5A_TRIANGLES_005.questionText: How many different triangles have sides that are whole numbers of centimetres and a perimeter of 13 cm? Triangles with the same three side lengths count as one triangle.
hints: Not every three numbers that add up to 13 make a triangle. Decide first how long the longest side is allowed to be.
The longest side must be shorter than the other two together, so it must be less than half of 13. It also cannot be less than 5 cm, or the three sides could not reach 13 cm.
A similar count for perimeter 9 cm: the longest side must be less than 4 and a half, so it is 3 or 4. That gives 3, 3, 3 and 4, 4, 1 and 4, 3, 2, which is 3 triangles.

stepByStep.text: The longest side must be less than the other two together, so it is less than half of 13 cm: at most 6 cm. It is at least 5 cm, because three sides of 4 cm or less cannot add up to 13 cm.
Longest side 6 cm: the other two add up to 7 cm, giving 6, 6, 1 and 6, 5, 2 and 6, 4, 3.
Longest side 5 cm: the other two add up to 8 cm, giving 5, 5, 3 and 5, 4, 4.
Count them: there are 5 triangles.

misconceptions.A: This counts every way of splitting 13 into three whole numbers, such as 1, 1, 11. Most of those cannot close up into a triangle.
misconceptions.B: Well done! With the longest side 6 cm there are three triangles and with 5 cm there are two, which makes 5.
misconceptions.C: These are the triangles with longest side 6 cm. The longest side can also be 5 cm.
misconceptions.D: Check the list for a repeat or for a set like 7, 3, 3, where the two shorter sides are too short to meet.

G5A_TRIANGLES_006.questionText: An isosceles triangle has sides that are whole numbers of centimetres and a perimeter of 20 cm. How many different triangles like this are there?
hints: Choose the length of the two equal sides and the third side is then fixed. But not every choice closes up into a triangle.
If each equal side is 3 cm, the third side is 14 cm. Can two sides of 3 cm reach across 14 cm? Find which lengths of the equal sides do work.
A similar count for perimeter 12 cm: equal sides of 4 cm give 4, 4, 4 and equal sides of 5 cm give 5, 5, 2. Equal sides of 3 cm give 3, 3, 6, which lies flat. So there are 2 triangles.

stepByStep.text: If each equal side is a certain length, the third side is 20 cm less twice that length.
The two equal sides together must be longer than the third side, so together they are more than half of 20 cm: each equal side is more than 5 cm.
The third side must be at least 1 cm, so each equal side is at most 9 cm.
The equal sides can be 6, 7, 8 or 9 cm, giving 6, 6, 8 and 7, 7, 6 and 8, 8, 4 and 9, 9, 2: that is 4 triangles.

misconceptions.A: This lets the equal sides be anything from 1 cm to 9 cm. Try 2, 2, 16: the two short sides cannot meet.
misconceptions.B: This counts 5, 5, 10 as well. There the two equal sides together exactly equal the third, so they lie flat along it.
misconceptions.C: Check each one by adding the two equal sides and comparing with the third side. Sets like 4, 4, 12 do not close up.
misconceptions.D: Well done! The equal sides can be 6, 7, 8 or 9 cm, which gives 4 triangles.

G5A_TRIANGLES_007.questionText: One angle of an isosceles triangle is 40°. Which answer gives every possible size of the largest angle of the triangle?
hints: An isosceles triangle has two equal angles. The question does not say whether the 40° angle is one of the equal pair or the odd one out.
First let 40° be one of the two equal angles and find the third angle. Then let 40° be the odd one out and find the two equal angles.
A similar triangle: one angle of an isosceles triangle is 50°. If the equal angles are 50° each, the third is 80°. If 50° is the odd one, the others are 65° each. So the largest angle is 65° or 80°.

stepByStep.text: If 40° is one of the two equal angles, the third angle is what is left.
If 40° is the odd one out, the two equal angles share the rest.
Halve it to find each equal angle.
The triangle is 40°, 40°, 100° or 40°, 70°, 70°, so its largest angle is 70° or 100°.

misconceptions.A: That is right when 40° is one of the equal angles. The 40° angle could also be the odd one out, with two equal angles beside it.
misconceptions.B: That is right when 40° is the odd one out. The 40° angle could also be one of the two equal angles.
misconceptions.C: Well done! The triangle can be 40°, 40°, 100° or 40°, 70°, 70°, so the largest angle is 70° or 100°.
misconceptions.D: 100° is one possibility. In the other triangle the angles are 40°, 70° and 70°, and its largest angle is not 40°.

G5A_TRIANGLES_008.questionText: Two sides of an isosceles triangle are 4 cm and 9 cm long. What is the perimeter of the triangle?
hints: The third side must equal one of the two given sides. Before adding up, check that each choice really makes a triangle.
Try the third side as 4 cm: can sides of 4 cm and 4 cm reach across a side of 9 cm? Then try the third side as 9 cm.
A similar triangle: an isosceles triangle has sides 3 cm and 8 cm. Sides 3, 3, 8 cannot meet, because 3 + 3 is less than 8. So the sides are 3, 8, 8 and the perimeter is 19 cm.

stepByStep.text: The third side is equal to one of the others, so it is 4 cm or 9 cm.
With 4 cm, 4 cm and 9 cm: 4 + 4 = 8, which is less than 9, so these sides cannot meet to make a triangle.
With 4 cm, 9 cm and 9 cm: 4 + 9 is more than 9, so this triangle can be made.
Add the three sides: the perimeter is 22 cm.

misconceptions.A: Well done! Only 4 cm, 9 cm, 9 cm closes up into a triangle, so the perimeter is 22 cm.
misconceptions.B: It is good to think of both choices, but test them: two sides of 4 cm together are only 8 cm and cannot reach across 9 cm.
misconceptions.C: This uses 4 cm, 4 cm and 9 cm. The two short sides together are only 8 cm, so their ends cannot meet.
misconceptions.D: This adds only the two given sides. A triangle has three sides, and the third equals one of the others.

G5A_TRIANGLES_009.questionText: One exterior angle of a triangle is 110°. Of the two interior angles that are not next to this exterior angle, one is 20° bigger than the other. What is the largest interior angle of the triangle?
hints: A triangle has three interior angles. Make sure you know all three before deciding which is the largest.
An exterior angle equals the two far interior angles added together, so those two add up to 110°. The interior angle next to the exterior angle lies with it on a straight line.
A similar triangle: an exterior angle is 100° and the two far interior angles differ by 10°, so they are 45° and 55°. The interior angle next to the exterior angle is 80°, and that is the largest.

stepByStep.text: The two far interior angles add up to the exterior angle, 110°, and one is 20° more than the other.
Take away the extra 20° and halve to find the smaller one.
So those two angles are 45° and 65°.
The third interior angle lies beside the exterior angle on a straight line.
The interior angles are 45°, 65° and 70°, so the largest interior angle is 70°.

misconceptions.A: 65° is the bigger of the two far angles. There is a third interior angle, next to the exterior angle: find it before choosing.
misconceptions.B: 110° is the exterior angle, which lies outside the triangle. The question asks for the largest interior angle.
misconceptions.C: 45° is the smallest interior angle. Find all three interior angles and pick the largest.
misconceptions.D: Well done! The interior angles are 45°, 65° and 70°, so the largest is 70°.

G5A_TRIANGLES_010.questionText: In a triangle, the largest angle is equal to the sum of the other two angles. One of those two angles is 4 times the other. What is the smallest angle of the triangle?
hints: Begin with the first sentence alone. If one angle equals the other two added together, what part of the whole 180° must it be?
The largest angle and the other two together make 180°, and the other two together equal the largest. So the largest angle is half of 180°.

A similar triangle: the largest angle equals the sum of the other two, and one of those is twice the other. The largest is 90°, and the other two share 90° as 1 part and 2 parts, so they are 30° and 60°.

stepByStep.text: The largest angle equals the other two together, so it is half of the total.
The other two angles add up to 90°, and one is 4 times the other, so together they are 5 equal parts.
Find one part.
The angles are 18°, 72° and 90°, so the smallest angle is 18°.

misconceptions.A: This shares all 180° between the two smaller angles. They add up only to the largest angle, which is half of 180°.
misconceptions.B: Well done! The largest angle is 90°, and the other two share 90° as 18° and 72°, so the smallest is 18°.
misconceptions.C: This shares 180° into 6 parts. Find the largest angle first: it equals the other two together, so it is 90°.
misconceptions.D: 72° is the middle angle, 4 times the smallest. The question asks for the smallest angle.

G5A_TRIANGLES_011.questionText: At each corner of a triangle, one exterior angle is drawn. What is the smallest number of these three exterior angles that can be obtuse?
hints: An exterior angle and the interior angle beside it lie on a straight line. Think about what kind of interior angle gives an obtuse exterior angle.
If an interior angle is acute, the exterior angle beside it is more than 90°. Now ask how many acute angles a triangle must have.
A similar idea: a triangle with interior angles 100°, 50° and 30° has exterior angles 80°, 130° and 150°. Only the corner with the obtuse interior angle has an acute exterior angle.

stepByStep.text: An exterior angle is 180° less the interior angle beside it, so it is obtuse exactly when that interior angle is acute.
A triangle cannot have two angles of 90° or more, because those two alone would already reach 180°.
So every triangle has at least two acute interior angles, and each of them gives an obtuse exterior angle.
A triangle such as 100°, 50°, 30° has exactly two obtuse exterior angles, so the smallest number is 2.

misconceptions.A: One is the greatest number of obtuse interior angles a triangle can have. Exterior angles work the other way round: acute inside means obtuse outside.
misconceptions.B: Lovely reasoning! Every triangle has at least two acute interior angles, and each gives an obtuse exterior angle, so the smallest number is 2.
misconceptions.C: For no exterior angle to be obtuse, every interior angle would have to be 90° or more, and three such angles add up to far more than 180°.
misconceptions.D: An acute-angled triangle does have 3 obtuse exterior angles, but the question asks for the smallest number. Try a triangle with an obtuse interior angle.

G5A_TRIANGLES_012.questionText: A triangle has a base of 20 cm, and the height drawn to that base is 9 cm. Another side of the same triangle is 12 cm long. What is the height drawn to the 12 cm side?
hints: Any side of a triangle can be used as the base, with its own height. Think about what stays the same whichever side you choose.
Use the first base and height to find the area: half of 20 × 9. The 12 cm side and its height must give the same area.

A similar triangle has base 10 cm with height 6 cm, so its area is 30 square centimetres. If another side is 8 cm, then half of 8 times its height is 30, so 4 times the height is 30 and the height is 7 and a half centimetres.

stepByStep.text: Find the area using the first base and height.
The area is 90 square centimetres whichever side is used as the base.
With the 12 cm side as base, half of 12 times the height is 90, so 12 times the height is 180.
Divide by 12: the height drawn to the 12 cm side is 15 cm.

misconceptions.A: This divides the area by 12. The area is half of base times height, so base times height is 180, not 90.
misconceptions.B: This makes the height smaller because the side is smaller. For the same area, a shorter base needs a taller height.
misconceptions.C: This doubles once too often. Base times height is twice the area, which is 180, and 180 ÷ 12 gives the height.
misconceptions.D: Well done! The area is 90 square centimetres, so 12 times the height is 180 and the height is 15 cm.

G5A_TRIANGLES_013.questionText: A triangle has sides that are whole numbers of centimetres and a perimeter of 24 cm. What is the greatest possible length of its longest side?
hints: When one side gets longer, the other two together get shorter, because the perimeter is fixed. Find the point where they can no longer meet.
If the longest side is 12 cm, the other two sides together are also 12 cm. Can they rise above the long side to make a triangle?
A similar triangle with perimeter 16 cm: a longest side of 8 cm leaves 8 cm for the other two, which would lie flat. A longest side of 7 cm leaves 9 cm, and 7, 7, 2 works. So the greatest is 7 cm.

stepByStep.text: The longest side must be shorter than the other two sides together.
A longest side of 12 cm leaves exactly 12 cm for the other two, so they would lie flat along it and make no triangle.
A longest side of 11 cm leaves 13 cm for the other two, which is more than 11 cm. For example, 11 cm, 11 cm and 2 cm make a triangle.
So the greatest possible length of the longest side is 11 cm.

misconceptions.A: Well done! The longest side must be less than half of 24 cm, and 11 cm works with sides such as 11, 11 and 2.
misconceptions.B: With a side of 12 cm the other two sides together are exactly 12 cm, so they lie flat along it. The longest side must be a little less.
misconceptions.C: Sides of 22 cm, 1 cm and 1 cm do add up to 24 cm, but the two short sides could never reach each other.
misconceptions.D: 8 cm is the side of the triangle with all sides equal. Other triangles with this perimeter have a longer longest side.

G5A_VARIATION_001.questionText: Asha and Bina collect stickers. The numbers of stickers they have are in the ratio 5 : 3. Asha gives 12 of her stickers to Bina, and now the two girls have the same number of stickers. How many stickers did Asha have at first?
hints: When one friend gives to the other, the total does not change, but the gap between them closes from both sides.
Asha has 5 parts and Bina has 3 parts, so the gap is 2 parts. Giving 12 stickers closes a gap that is twice as big as 12.

Similar problem: two boys have marbles in the ratio 7 : 3. The first gives 10 marbles to the second and they become equal. The gap was 2 × 10 = 20 marbles, which is 4 parts, so one part is 5 and the first boy had 7 × 5 = 35 marbles.

stepByStep.text: Giving 12 stickers takes Asha down by 12 and Bina up by 12, so the gap between them was 24.
The gap is 5 − 3 = 2 parts, so one part is 12 stickers.
Asha had 5 parts.
Check: 60 and 36 become 48 and 48. Asha had 60 stickers at first.

misconceptions.A: This comes from treating the 12 stickers as the whole gap of 2 parts. The gap closes from both sides, so it was really 24 stickers.
misconceptions.B: Yes! The gap of 2 parts is 24 stickers, so one part is 12 and Asha's 5 parts make 60.
misconceptions.C: 36 is the number Bina had at first. The question asks for Asha, who has 5 parts.
misconceptions.D: 96 is the total of both girls together. Asha's share is 5 of the 8 parts.

G5A_VARIATION_002.questionText: Meena and Tara share some money in the ratio 5 : 1. Meena then gives ₹15 to Tara, and the ratio of Meena's money to Tara's money becomes 2 : 1. How much money does Meena have now?
hints: The total money stays the same when one person gives to the other. Make both ratios describe the same total number of parts.
5 : 1 has 6 parts in all, but 2 : 1 has only 3. Rewrite 2 : 1 as 4 : 2 so that both ratios have 6 parts.

Similar problem: two friends have money in the ratio 3 : 1. The first gives ₹8 to the second and the ratio becomes 1 : 1, which is 2 : 2 with the same 4 parts. The first went from 3 parts to 2 parts, so one part is ₹8 and the first now has 2 × 8 = ₹16.

stepByStep.text: The total does not change. 5 : 1 is 6 parts, so write the new ratio 2 : 1 as 4 : 2, which is also 6 parts.
Meena goes from 5 parts to 4 parts, so one part is the ₹15 she gave.
Meena now has 4 parts.
Check: ₹75 and ₹15 become ₹60 and ₹30, which is 2 : 1. Meena has ₹60 now.

misconceptions.A: This treats the parts in 5 : 1 and 2 : 1 as the same size, so that 3 parts would be ₹15. The parts only match once both ratios have the same total.
misconceptions.B: ₹75 is what Meena had before giving. Take away the ₹15 she gave to Tara.
misconceptions.C: Well done! With both ratios written in 6 parts, one part is ₹15 and Meena's 4 parts are ₹60.
misconceptions.D: ₹30 is what Tara has now. The question asks about Meena.

G5A_VARIATION_003.questionText: In a chess club the ratio of boys to girls is 3 : 4. Then 6 more boys join, and no girls join or leave. The ratio of boys to girls becomes 6 : 7. How many children are in the club now?
hints: The number of girls does not change, so make the girls' part the same number in both ratios.
Girls are 4 parts in the first ratio and 7 parts in the second. Rewrite both ratios so that the girls are 28 parts.

Similar problem: red to blue beads are 2 : 3. After 4 more red beads are added the ratio is 5 : 6. With blue as 6 parts both times, the ratios are 4 : 6 and 5 : 6, so one part is 4 beads and there are now 11 × 4 = 44 beads.

stepByStep.text: The number of girls stays the same, so write both ratios with the girls as 28 parts: 3 : 4 = 21 : 28 and 6 : 7 = 24 : 28.
Boys go from 21 parts to 24 parts. These 3 parts are the 6 new boys, so one part is 2 children.
Now there are 24 + 28 = 52 parts.
There are 104 children in the club now.

misconceptions.A: This takes 6 − 3 = 3 parts straight from the two ratios, but those parts are not the same size. First make the girls' parts equal in both ratios.
misconceptions.B: 98 is the number of children before the 6 boys joined. Add the new boys.
misconceptions.C: 56 is the number of girls only. Add the boys as well.
misconceptions.D: Great thinking! With the girls fixed at 28 parts, one part is 2 children and 52 parts make 104.

G5A_VARIATION_004.questionText: In Class 5B, the ratio of the children who walk to school to ALL the children in the class is 3 : 8. There are 40 children who do not walk to school. How many children walk to school?
hints: Check what the second number in the ratio stands for: is it another group, or the whole class?
Out of every 8 children, 3 walk, so 8 − 3 = 5 do not walk. The 40 children match those 5 parts.
Similar problem: the ratio of red balloons to all the balloons is 2 : 7, and 30 balloons are not red. Not red is 7 − 2 = 5 parts, so one part is 6 and there are 2 × 6 = 12 red balloons.

stepByStep.text: The ratio compares the walkers with the whole class: 3 parts walk out of 8 parts in all.
So 8 − 3 = 5 parts do not walk, and these are the 40 children.
The walkers are 3 parts.
24 children walk to school.

misconceptions.A: Yes! The 40 children are the 5 parts that do not walk, so one part is 8 and 3 parts are 24.
misconceptions.B: This reads 3 : 8 as walkers to non-walkers. The 8 stands for the whole class, so the non-walkers are 5 parts.
misconceptions.C: 64 is the whole class. The question asks only for the children who walk.
misconceptions.D: This takes 5 parts out of 8 from the 40 children, but the 40 are already the 5 parts. Find one part first.

G5A_VARIATION_005.questionText: Anu, Bela and Chitra share ₹372. Anu's share to Bela's share is 3 : 4, and Bela's share to Chitra's share is 6 : 5. How much does Chitra get?
hints: Bela appears in both ratios. Make Bela's number the same in both before joining them into one ratio.
Bela is 4 in one ratio and 6 in the other. Change both ratios so that Bela is 12.
Similar problem: P to Q is 1 : 2 and Q to R is 3 : 4, and they share ₹170. With Q as 6, the ratios are 3 : 6 and 6 : 8, so P : Q : R = 3 : 6 : 8. That is 17 parts of ₹10 each, so R gets 8 × 10 = ₹80.

stepByStep.text: Bela must have the same number in both ratios: 3 : 4 = 9 : 12 and 6 : 5 = 12 : 10.
So Anu : Bela : Chitra = 9 : 12 : 10, which is 31 parts.
One part is ₹12.
Chitra gets 10 parts, which is ₹120.

misconceptions.A: This joins the ratios as 3 : 4 : 5 without matching Bela's two numbers, 4 and 6. Make Bela 12 in both ratios first.
misconceptions.B: Well done! The joined ratio is 9 : 12 : 10, one part is ₹12 and Chitra's 10 parts are ₹120.
misconceptions.C: ₹108 is Anu's share of 9 parts. Chitra has 10 parts.
misconceptions.D: ₹144 is Bela's share of 12 parts. Chitra has 10 parts.

G5A_VARIATION_006.questionText: Half of Kavi's savings is equal to one-third of Lata's savings. Together they have saved ₹150. How much has Kavi saved?
hints: If half of one amount equals only a third of another amount, think about which of the two amounts must be larger.
Call the equal amount one block. Kavi's savings are 2 blocks, because half of them is 1 block. How many blocks are Lata's savings?
Similar problem: one-third of Raj's marbles equals one-quarter of Sam's marbles, and together they have 70. Raj has 3 blocks and Sam has 4 blocks, so one block is 10 and Raj has 30 marbles.

stepByStep.text: Call the equal amount 1 block. Half of Kavi's savings is 1 block, so Kavi has 2 blocks.
One-third of Lata's savings is 1 block, so Lata has 3 blocks.
Together they have 5 blocks worth ₹150, so one block is ₹30.
Kavi has 2 blocks, which is ₹60.

misconceptions.A: This shares ₹150 as 3 : 2 in Kavi's favour. But half of Kavi's money matches only a third of Lata's, so Lata must have more: the ratio is 2 : 3.
misconceptions.B: ₹75 is an equal split. Their savings are not equal, because half of one matches a third of the other.
misconceptions.C: Lovely reasoning! Kavi has 2 blocks and Lata has 3 blocks, so Kavi's share is ₹60.
misconceptions.D: ₹100 is two-thirds of the total. Count blocks instead: Kavi has 2 and Lata has 3, so Kavi has 2 of the 5 blocks.

G5A_VARIATION_007.questionText: 12 workers can build a wall in 20 days. They all work for 5 days, and then 3 of the workers leave. The others finish the wall at the same pace. How many days does the wall take from start to finish?
hints: Measure the whole job in worker-days: the work one worker does in one day.
The wall needs 12 × 20 worker-days. Find how many of them are used up in the first 5 days.

Similar problem: 10 workers need 12 days. After 2 days, 5 of them leave. The job is 120 worker-days, 20 are done, and 100 are left for 5 workers, which takes 20 more days. From start to finish that is 2 + 20 = 22 days.

stepByStep.text: The whole wall is 240 worker-days of work.
In the first 5 days, 12 workers do 60 worker-days, so 180 are left.
Now 9 workers remain, so they need 20 more days.
From start to finish the wall takes 25 days.

misconceptions.A: 20 days is how long the 9 workers need after the others leave. Add the 5 days already worked.
misconceptions.B: 15 days would be left if nobody had gone. With only 9 workers the remaining work takes longer.
misconceptions.C: Losing 3 workers does not simply add 3 days. Count the work left in worker-days and share it among 9 workers.
misconceptions.D: Excellent! 180 worker-days are left for 9 workers, which is 20 more days, so 25 days in all.

G5A_VARIATION_008.questionText: A hostel has enough rice to feed 40 students for 30 days. After 10 days, 10 more students join the hostel. For how many more days will the rice last?
hints: Count the rice in student-days: the rice one student eats in one day. First work out how much is left when the new students arrive.
After 10 days, the 40 students still have rice for 20 days. How many student-days of rice is that?
Similar problem: food lasts 20 campers for 15 days. After 5 days, 5 more campers come. The food left is 20 × 10 = 200 camper-days, and 25 campers finish it in 8 days.

stepByStep.text: After 10 days, the rice left would feed 40 students for 20 more days.
That is 800 student-days of rice.
Now there are 50 students.
The rice will last 16 more days.

misconceptions.A: Yes! 800 student-days of rice are left, and 50 students use them up in 16 days.
misconceptions.B: This shares all 30 days of rice among 50 students, but 10 days of rice had already been eaten before the new students came.
misconceptions.C: This finds 24 days for 50 students and then takes away 10. The first 10 days were eaten by only 40 students, so start from the rice that is left.
misconceptions.D: 20 days is how long the rice would last if nobody joined. With more students it runs out sooner.

G5A_VARIATION_009.questionText: A taxi charges a fixed amount for every trip plus the same amount for each kilometre. A 5 km trip costs ₹110 and an 8 km trip costs ₹155. How much does a 12 km trip cost?
hints: Because of the fixed amount, the cost is not simply so many rupees per kilometre. Compare the two trips to see what the extra kilometres cost.
The 8 km trip is 3 km longer than the 5 km trip and costs ₹45 more. What does each extra kilometre cost?
Similar problem: a cab costs ₹70 for 2 km and ₹110 for 6 km. The extra 4 km cost ₹40, so each kilometre is ₹10 and the fixed amount is ₹50. A 10 km trip costs 50 + 100 = ₹150.

stepByStep.text: The extra 3 km cost ₹45, so each kilometre costs ₹15.
For 5 km the kilometres cost ₹75, so the fixed amount is ₹35.
12 km cost ₹180 for the kilometres.
Adding the fixed amount, the 12 km trip costs ₹215.

misconceptions.A: This uses ₹110 ÷ 5 = ₹22 for every kilometre. Part of the ₹110 is the fixed amount, so compare the two trips first.
misconceptions.B: Well done! Each kilometre costs ₹15 and the fixed amount is ₹35, so 12 km cost ₹215.
misconceptions.C: ₹180 pays for the kilometres only. Add the fixed amount for the trip.
misconceptions.D: This adds the two fares together. Find the cost of one kilometre and the fixed amount instead.

G5A_VARIATION_010.questionText: A 30-litre mixture has milk and water in the ratio 7 : 3. How many litres of water must be added so that the ratio of milk to water becomes 3 : 2?
hints: Only water is added, so the amount of milk stays the same. Build the new ratio around the milk.
First find the litres of milk and of water in the 30 litres: 7 parts and 3 parts out of 10 parts.

Similar problem: 40 litres of juice and water are in the ratio 3 : 1, so there are 30 litres of juice and 10 litres of water. For a ratio of 3 : 2 with 30 litres of juice, the water must be 20 litres, so 10 litres of water are added.

stepByStep.text: One part is 3 litres, so there are 21 litres of milk and 9 litres of water.
The milk stays at 21 litres. In the ratio 3 : 2 the milk is 3 parts, so one part is 7 litres.
The water must be 2 parts, which is 14 litres.
Water to add: 5 litres.

misconceptions.A: This splits 30 litres as 3 : 2, but the mixture grows when water is added. Keep the milk at 21 litres and build the new ratio from it.
misconceptions.B: 14 litres is the water needed in all. There are already 9 litres in the mixture.
misconceptions.C: Yes! The milk stays at 21 litres, so the water must be 14 litres, and 5 more litres are needed.
misconceptions.D: 12 litres would be the water if the mixture stayed at 30 litres. The total grows, so work from the 21 litres of milk.

G5A_VARIATION_011.questionText: Jar P holds 20 litres of milk and water mixed in the ratio 3 : 1. Jar Q holds 30 litres of milk and water mixed in the ratio 2 : 3. Both jars are emptied into one big drum. What is the ratio of milk to water in the drum?
hints: Ratios cannot be added directly when the jars hold different amounts. Work in litres.
Find the litres of milk and of water in Jar P: 3 parts and 1 part out of 20 litres.

Similar problem: 10 litres mixed 4 : 1 has 8 litres of milk and 2 litres of water. 20 litres mixed 1 : 1 has 10 litres of each. Together that is 18 litres of milk and 12 litres of water, a ratio of 3 : 2.

stepByStep.text: Jar P: 4 parts are 20 litres, so it has 15 litres of milk and 5 litres of water.
Jar Q: 5 parts are 30 litres, so it has 12 litres of milk and 18 litres of water.
In the drum there are 15 + 12 = 27 litres of milk and 5 + 18 = 23 litres of water.
The ratio of milk to water in the drum is 27 : 23.

misconceptions.A: This adds the ratio numbers, 3 + 2 and 1 + 3. The jars hold different amounts, so change each ratio into litres first.
misconceptions.B: These are the right litres, but in the order water to milk. The question asks for milk to water.
misconceptions.C: This compares the milk with everything in the drum. Compare the milk with the water instead.
misconceptions.D: Well done! The drum has 27 litres of milk and 23 litres of water.

G5A_VARIATION_012.questionText: A money box has only ₹1, ₹2 and ₹5 coins. The numbers of ₹1, ₹2 and ₹5 coins are in the ratio 5 : 3 : 2. The total value of all the coins is ₹210. How many ₹5 coins are in the box?
hints: The ratio counts coins, but ₹210 is a value. Find the value of one small group of coins first.
Take one group of 5 one-rupee coins, 3 two-rupee coins and 2 five-rupee coins. How many rupees is this group worth?
Similar problem: ₹1 and ₹5 coins are in the ratio 3 : 1 and are worth ₹64 in all. One group of 3 one-rupee coins and 1 five-rupee coin is worth ₹8, so there are 8 groups and 8 five-rupee coins.

stepByStep.text: One group has 5 coins of ₹1, 3 coins of ₹2 and 2 coins of ₹5. It is worth ₹21.
The number of such groups is 10.
Each group has 2 coins of ₹5.
There are 20 five-rupee coins in the box.

misconceptions.A: Yes! One group of coins is worth ₹21, so there are 10 groups and 20 five-rupee coins.
misconceptions.B: This shares ₹210 in the ratio 5 : 3 : 2. The ratio tells how many coins there are, and the coins have different values.
misconceptions.C: 10 is the number of groups. Each group has 2 five-rupee coins.
misconceptions.D: ₹100 is the value of the five-rupee coins. The question asks how many of them there are.

G5A_VARIATION_013.questionText: The ages of a mother and her daughter Riya are in the ratio 7 : 2. In 5 years' time, their ages will be in the ratio 8 : 3. How old is the mother now?
hints: Both of them grow older by the same number of years, so the difference between their ages never changes.
In 7 : 2 the difference is 5 parts, and in 8 : 3 the difference is also 5 parts. So the parts are the same size in both ratios.

Similar problem: a father's and a son's ages are in the ratio 5 : 1. In 6 years they will be in the ratio 3 : 1, which is 6 : 2. The difference is 4 parts both times, so one part is 6 years and the father is 5 × 6 = 30 now.

stepByStep.text: The difference in ages stays the same. It is 7 − 2 = 5 parts now and 8 − 3 = 5 parts later, so the parts are the same size.
The mother goes from 7 parts to 8 parts in 5 years, so one part is 5 years.
The mother is 7 parts now.
Check: 35 and 10 become 40 and 15, which is 8 : 3. The mother is 35 years old now.

misconceptions.A: 40 is the mother's age in 5 years' time, when the ratio is 8 : 3. The question asks for her age now.
misconceptions.B: Well done! One part is 5 years, so the mother is 35 and Riya is 10.
misconceptions.C: If the mother were 28, Riya would be 8, and in 5 years they would be 33 and 13, which is not 8 : 3. Use the fact that the age gap stays the same.
misconceptions.D: If the mother were 42, Riya would be 12, and in 5 years they would be 47 and 17, which is not 8 : 3. Use the fact that the age gap stays the same.

G5A_VARIATION_014.questionText: 3 men or 6 boys can paint a school hall in 20 days. How many days will 2 men and 4 boys take to paint the same hall, working together?
hints: Change all the workers into one kind first, so that the whole team is counted in the same unit.
3 men do the same work as 6 boys, so 1 man works like 2 boys. How many boys is the team of 2 men and 4 boys worth?
Similar problem: 2 men or 6 boys finish a job in 12 days. One man equals 3 boys, so 1 man and 6 boys equal 9 boys. The job is 6 × 12 = 72 boy-days, so they take 8 days.

stepByStep.text: 3 men do the work of 6 boys, so 1 man does the work of 2 boys.
2 men and 4 boys are like 4 + 4 = 8 boys.
The hall needs 120 boy-days of work.
8 boys take 15 days.

misconceptions.A: This counts 2 men and 4 boys as 6 workers, the same as 6 boys. A man does twice the work of a boy, so the team is worth 8 boys.
misconceptions.B: 10 days is the time for 3 men and 6 boys all working together. This team is 2 men and 4 boys.
misconceptions.C: Yes! The team is worth 8 boys, and 120 boy-days of work take them 15 days.
misconceptions.D: 30 days is the time for the 2 men alone. The 4 boys are helping too.

G5A_VARIATION_015.questionText: Kiran and Leela had money in the ratio 3 : 2. Each of them spent ₹40 on a book. Now the ratio of Kiran's money to Leela's money is 2 : 1. How much money did Kiran have at first?
hints: Both spend the same amount, so the difference between their money does not change.
In 3 : 2 the difference is 1 part, and in 2 : 1 the difference is also 1 part. So the parts are the same size before and after.

Similar problem: two friends have money in the ratio 5 : 3. Each spends ₹30 and the ratio becomes 2 : 1, which is 4 : 2. The gap is 2 parts both times, so each friend lost 1 part. One part is ₹30 and the first friend had 5 × 30 = ₹150.

stepByStep.text: Both spend ₹40, so the difference stays the same: 1 part before and 1 part after. The parts are the same size.
Kiran goes from 3 parts to 2 parts, so one part is the ₹40 he spent.
At first Kiran had 3 parts.
Check: ₹120 and ₹80 become ₹80 and ₹40, which is 2 : 1. Kiran had ₹120 at first.

misconceptions.A: ₹80 is what Kiran has after buying the book. Add back the ₹40 he spent.
misconceptions.B: ₹200 is the total the two friends had at first. Kiran's share is 3 of the 5 parts.
misconceptions.C: This takes one part as ₹20. Kiran drops from 3 parts to 2 parts by spending ₹40, so one part is ₹40.
misconceptions.D: Great! One part is ₹40, so Kiran had 3 parts, which is ₹120.
